papers.research_question: How can we understand and measure the linguistic competence of large language models with respect to their representation and use of human-interpretable linguistic properties?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the CALM framework for analyzing LLM competence using causal probing and develops Gradient-Based Interventions (GBIs), a novel causal probing method that can target arbitrarily-encoded representations.
papers.conclusion: CALM and GBIs provide an effective framework and methodology for analyzing LLM competence, explaining behavioral patterns across lexical inference tasks.
papers.key_findings:
BERT and RoBERTa are partially competent on lexical inference tasks, with BERT generally more competent than RoBERTa.
Competence scores correlate with task performance, providing an explanation for brittle performance under prompt variation.
Gradient-Based Interventions enable causal probing of a broader range of representations than prior techniques.
papers.limitation:
Gradient-Based Interventions face a tradeoff between completeness (manipulating the target property) and selectivity (avoiding damage to non-target properties).
Probes may leverage spurious information rather than the true representation of the target property.
Experiments are conducted on comparatively small, well-studied models (BERT and RoBERTa) and may not generalize to larger, more complex models.
future_direction: Scaling CALM to larger, more powerful models and more difficult tasks.
Studying the impact of model training and fine-tuning choices on learned representations.
Using CALM for multitask learning and understanding task dependencies.
Combining CALM with causal graph discovery algorithms to infer implicit task representations.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent successes of large, pretrained neural language models (LLMs), comparatively little is known about the representations of linguistic structure they learn during pretraining, which can lead to unexpected behaviors in response to prompt variation or distribution shift. To better understand these models and behaviors, we introduce a general model analysis framework to study LLMs with respect to their representation and use of human-interpretable linguistic properties. Our framework, CALM (Competence-based Analysis of Language Models), is designed to investigate LLM competence in the context of specific tasks by intervening on models' internal representations of different linguistic properties using causal probing, and measuring models' alignment under these interventions with a given ground-truth causal model of the task. We also develop a new approach for performing causal probing interventions using gradient-based adversarial attacks, which can target a broader range of properties and representations than prior techniques. Finally, we carry out a case study of CALM using these interventions to analyze and compare LLM competence across a variety of lexical inference tasks, showing that CALM can be used to explain behaviors across these tasks.

papers.title: Inside-Out: Hidden Factual Knowledge in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does LLMs encode more factual knowledge in their parameters than they express in their outputs?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a formal framework to define and measure hidden factual knowledge in LLMs, demonstrating that LLMs encode more knowledge internally than they express externally.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents evidence of hidden knowledge in LLMs and calls for methods to surface internal knowledge more effectively for transparent and reliable models.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs consistently encode more factual knowledge internally than externally, with an average relative gap of 40%.
Some knowledge is so hidden that models can internally know an answer perfectly yet fail to generate it even after 1000 sampling attempts.
This reveals fundamental limitations in the generation capabilities of LLMs and constraints on scaling test-time compute.
papers.limitation: Results are a lower bound because only a single internal scoring function (probing) is used.
future_direction: Understanding reasons for differences in hidden knowledge across models
Developing methods to surface internal knowledge more effectively
papers.abstract: This work presents a framework for assessing whether large language models (LLMs) encode more factual knowledge in their parameters than what they express in their outputs. While a few studies hint at this possibility, none has clearly defined or demonstrated this phenomenon. We first propose a formal definition of knowledge, quantifying it for a given question as the fraction of correct-incorrect answer pairs where the correct one is ranked higher. This gives rise to external and internal knowledge, depending on the information used to score individual answer candidates: either the model's observable token-level probabilities or its intermediate computations. Hidden knowledge arises when internal knowledge exceeds external knowledge. We then present a case study, applying this framework to three popular open-weights LLMs in a closed-book QA setup. Our results indicate that: (1) LLMs consistently encode more factual knowledge internally than what they express externally, with an average relative gap of 40%. (2) Surprisingly, some knowledge is so deeply hidden that a model can internally know an answer perfectly, yet fail to generate it even once, despite large-scale repeated sampling of 1,000 answers. This reveals fundamental limitations in the generation capabilities of LLMs, which (3) put a practical constraint on scaling test-time compute via repeated answer sampling in closed-book QA: significant performance improvements remain inaccessible because some answers are practically never sampled, yet if they were, we would be guaranteed to rank them first.

papers.title: Exploring Concept Depth: How Large Language Models Acquire Knowledge and Concept at Different Layers?
papers.research_question: Can shallow layers in LLMs capture meaningful features of simple knowledge, while complex concepts need deeper layers to capture their meaningful features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of 'Concept Depth' to measure how different layers in LLMs capture concepts of varying complexity, showing that simpler concepts are learned in shallow layers while complex concepts require deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: The Concept Depth metric provides a useful framework for understanding how LLMs process concepts of varying complexity across layers, and the experimental insights enhance the understanding of internal representations in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler concepts (e.g., factual knowledge) are learned in shallow layers, while more complex concepts (e.g., reasoning tasks) require deeper layers for accurate understanding.
The pattern of Concept Depth is consistent across different model families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) and model sizes.
Larger models within a family tend to achieve higher peak accuracy and sometimes converge to optimal performance at earlier layers.
Adding noise to the input or quantizing model weights (e.g., to 8-bit) slows down the convergence of concept understanding, requiring deeper layers to achieve comparable accuracy.
Compressing models to 16-bit quantization does not significantly harm the understanding process compared to 32-bit.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performances across a wide range of tasks. However, the mechanisms by which these models encode tasks of varying complexities remain poorly understood. In this paper, we explore the hypothesis that LLMs process concepts of varying complexities in different layers, introducing the idea of "Concept Depth" to suggest that more complex concepts are typically acquired in deeper layers. Specifically, we categorize concepts based on their level of abstraction, defining them in the order of increasing complexity within factual, emotional, and inferential tasks. We conduct extensive probing experiments using layer-wise representations across various LLM families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) on various datasets spanning the three domains of tasks. Our findings reveal that models could efficiently conduct probing for simpler tasks in shallow layers, and more complex tasks typically necessitate deeper layers for accurate understanding. Additionally, we examine how external factors, such as adding noise to the input and quantizing the model weights, might affect layer-wise representations. Our findings suggest that these factors can impede the development of a conceptual understanding of LLMs until deeper layers are explored. We hope that our proposed concept and experimental insights will enhance the understanding of the mechanisms underlying LLMs. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Luckfort/CD.

papers.title: Information Anxiety in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the effect of entity popularity on the internal reasoning and retrieval mechanisms of LLMs, and do queries about popular entities cause ambiguity or confusion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces 'information anxiety', a phenomenon where LLMs exhibit internal strains when processing highly popular queries, leading to rapid convergence of probability distributions but poor attention and inconsistent fact retrieval across lexical variations.
papers.conclusion: Information anxiety reveals vulnerabilities in LLMs' processing of prevalent information, emphasizing the need for robust evaluation and better pretraining data scrutiny.
papers.key_findings:
For highly popular questions, the predicted probability distribution converges earlier to the target distribution.
LLMs pay lower attention to constraint tokens in popular queries, indicating poor engagement with query details.
Retrieved facts across lexical variations become more dissimilar as query popularity increases, showing sensitivity to phrasing.
LLMs struggle to segregate facts from distinct relations for popular subjects, leading to higher inter-relation similarity.
Despite internal inconsistencies, LLMs remain confident in predictions for popular queries, as shown by high probability scores.
papers.limitation:
Entity and popularity formatted datasets like PopQA are hard to curate.
Developing better proxies for entity popularity in pretraining data is non-trivial.
Challenges in tracking and standardizing pretraining data quality due to volume and closed-source nature.
future_direction: Reducing sensitivity to lexical variations in knowledge queries.
Reducing popularity-dependent strains in internal mechanisms of LLMs.
Exploring alternative proxies for entity popularity in pretraining corpora.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance as knowledge repositories, enabling models to understand user queries and generate accurate and context-aware responses. Extensive evaluation setups have corroborated the positive correlation between the retrieval capability of LLMs and the frequency of entities in their pretraining corpus. We take the investigation further by conducting a comprehensive analysis of the internal reasoning and retrieval mechanisms of LLMs. Our work focuses on three critical dimensions - the impact of entity popularity, the models' sensitivity to lexical variations in query formulation, and the progression of hidden state representations across LLM layers. Our preliminary findings reveal that popular questions facilitate early convergence of internal states toward the correct answer. However, as the popularity of a query increases, retrieved attributes across lexical variations become increasingly dissimilar and less accurate. Interestingly, we find that LLMs struggle to disentangle facts, grounded in distinct relations, from their parametric memory when dealing with highly popular subjects. Through a case study, we explore these latent strains within LLMs when processing highly popular queries, a phenomenon we term information anxiety. The emergence of information anxiety in LLMs underscores the adversarial injection in the form of linguistic variations and calls for a more holistic evaluation of frequently occurring entities.

papers.title: Emergence of Linear Truth Encodings in Language Models
papers.research_question: Why and how do linear truth subspaces that separate true from false statements emerge in language models during training and inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that linear truth encodings in language models can emerge from the statistical co-occurrence of true/false statements (Truth Co-occurrence Hypothesis), demonstrated through a toy transformer model and experiments.
papers.conclusion: Linear truth encodings in language models can emerge from the co-occurrence statistics of true and false statements, as demonstrated by a toy model and supported by experiments in pretrained models.
papers.key_findings:
Linear truth encoding emerges in a one-layer transformer trained on data where true/false statements co-occur (Truth Co-occurrence Hypothesis).
Training exhibits two phases: fast memorization of factual associations followed by slower development of linear truth separation.
Layer normalization is necessary for the linear separability of true and false representations.
The value matrix develops a block structure that enables sharpening of predictions for true sequences.
Experiments with Pythia-6.9B show similar two-phase dynamics in a large pretrained model.
papers.limitation:
The toy model is far simpler than natural training data, so the mechanism might not fully capture real-world complexity.
In real LMs, additional mechanisms likely contribute to truth encoding.
future_direction: Systematic study of mechanisms for truth encoding in real LMs.
Generalization of truth encoding across different relations.
papers.abstract: Recent probing studies reveal that large language models exhibit linear subspaces that separate true from false statements, yet the mechanism behind their emergence is unclear. We introduce a transparent, one-layer transformer toy model that reproduces such truth subspaces end-to-end and exposes one concrete route by which they can arise. We study one simple setting in which truth encoding can emerge: a data distribution where factual statements co-occur with other factual statements (and vice-versa), encouraging the model to learn this distinction in order to lower the LM loss on future tokens. We corroborate this pattern with experiments in pretrained language models. Finally, in the toy setting we observe a two-phase learning dynamic: networks first memorize individual factual associations in a few steps, then -- over a longer horizon -- learn to linearly separate true from false, which in turn lowers language-modeling loss. Together, these results provide both a mechanistic demonstration and an empirical motivation for how and why linear truth representations can emerge in language models.

papers.title: Core Knowledge Deficits in Multi-Modal Language Models
papers.research_question: Do multi-modal large language models lack core knowledge, i.e., rudimentary cognitive abilities that are innate in humans from early childhood?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the CoreCognition benchmark for evaluating core knowledge in MLLMs and finds that MLLMs exhibit significant deficits in low-level core abilities, show misaligned dependencies between abilities, and rely on shortcut learning rather than genuine understanding as they scale.
papers.conclusion: MLLMs exhibit significant deficits in core knowledge, and scaling does not lead to genuine understanding but instead increases reliance on shortcut learning.
papers.key_findings:
MLLMs consistently perform worse on low-level core abilities compared to high-level abilities.
MLLM performance on high-level abilities is not correlated with the underlying low-level abilities that support them.
MLLMs exhibit less, or even no, scalability on low-level abilities compared to high-level abilities as model parameters increase.
Models increasing in size exhibit core deficits and shortcut-taking behaviors rather than progressing toward conceptual understanding.
The proposed Concept Hacking method reveals MLLMs fail to achieve genuine core knowledge understanding and instead rely on shortcut learning.
papers.abstract: While Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) demonstrate impressive abilities over high-level perception and reasoning, their robustness in the wild remains limited, often falling short on tasks that are intuitive and effortless for humans. We examine the hypothesis that these deficiencies stem from the absence of core knowledge--rudimentary cognitive abilities innate to humans from early childhood. To explore the core knowledge representation in MLLMs, we introduce CoreCognition, a large-scale benchmark encompassing 12 core knowledge concepts grounded in developmental cognitive science. We evaluate 230 models with 11 different prompts, leading to a total of 2,530 data points for analysis. Our experiments uncover four key findings, collectively demonstrating core knowledge deficits in MLLMs: they consistently underperform and show reduced, or even absent, scalability on low-level abilities relative to high-level ones. Finally, we propose Concept Hacking, a novel controlled evaluation method that reveals MLLMs fail to progress toward genuine core knowledge understanding, but instead rely on shortcut learning as they scale.

papers.title: Its Alive: AI Independence Without Human Prompting
papers.research_question: How can representation engineering (RepE) improve transparency and control of AI systems, particularly for safety-relevant concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces representation engineering (RepE) as a top-down approach to AI transparency, providing baselines like Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) and demonstrating its applicability to reading and controlling safety-relevant concepts in large language models.
papers.conclusion: RepE is a promising top-down approach for enhancing AI transparency and control, with broad applicability to safety-relevant problems, and can accelerate progress in AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
RepE methods can extract representations of high-level concepts like honesty, utility, emotion, and harmfulness.
LAT achieves state-of-the-art on TruthfulQA, improving zero-shot accuracy by 18.1 percentage points.
Representation control can increase model honesty and reduce compliance with harmful instructions, even under jailbreak attempts.
Emotions are represented in LLMs and can be manipulated to affect model compliance and behavior.
RepE provides traction on inner alignment problems like deceptive alignment by enabling monitoring and control of honesty.
future_direction: Further exploration of RepE for transparency and safety of AI systems.
Investigation of emotion representations and their impact on model behavior and concept of self.
Improving robustness and generalization of RepE methods.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify and characterize the emerging area of representation engineering (RepE), an approach to enhancing the transparency of AI systems that draws on insights from cognitive neuroscience. RepE places population-level representations, rather than neurons or circuits, at the center of analysis, equipping us with novel methods for monitoring and manipulating high-level cognitive phenomena in deep neural networks (DNNs). We provide baselines and an initial analysis of RepE techniques, showing that they offer simple yet effective solutions for improving our understanding and control of large language models. We showcase how these methods can provide traction on a wide range of safety-relevant problems, including honesty, harmlessness, power-seeking, and more, demonstrating the promise of top-down transparency research. We hope that this work catalyzes further exploration of RepE and fosters advancements in the transparency and safety of AI systems.

papers.title: The Shape of Beliefs: Geometry, Dynamics, and Interventions along Representation Manifolds of Language Models' Posteriors
papers.research_question: How are prompt-conditioned beliefs encoded in representation space, how do they update with new evidence, and how can interventions reshape them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that beliefs in LLMs are encoded as curved manifolds in representation space, and that linear steering often fails to preserve the intended belief family, while geometry-aware steering based on linear field probes is more effective.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that rich structure emerges naturally in LLMs and that purely linear concept representations are often an inadequate abstraction, highlighting the importance of geometry-aware methods for interpretability and intervention.
papers.key_findings:
Belief manifolds for distribution parameters (mean and standard deviation) are curved in representation space.
Linear field probes can tile the manifold and decode parameters with high accuracy and smooth variation.
When the input distribution changes, the model updates its beliefs along trajectories on the manifold, with different timescales for mean and variance.
Linear steering can push activations off-manifold, causing coupled shifts in other parameters (e.g., variance).
Geometry-aware steering using linear field probes better preserves the intended belief family and avoids unintended coupled shifts.
papers.limitation:
Relies on small open-source base models and focuses on a restricted family of prompt distributions (time-series), which may not capture the diversity of internal geometries in other settings.
The assumption that beliefs live on manifolds indexable by interpretable parameters may not hold in natural language tasks where latent variables are not fully parameterizable.
Does not investigate causal attribution to uncover which neuronal structure or circuits are responsible for the observed geometry.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) represent prompt-conditioned beliefs (posteriors over answers and claims), but we lack a mechanistic account of how these beliefs are encoded in representation space, how they update with new evidence, and how interventions reshape them. We study a controlled setting in which Llama-3.2 generates samples from a normal distribution by implicitly inferring its parameters (mean and standard deviation) given only samples from the distribution in context. We find representations of curved "belief manifolds" for these parameters form with sufficient in-context learning and study how the model adapts when the distribution suddenly changes. While standard linear steering often pushes the model off-manifold and induces coupled, out-of-distribution shifts, geometry and field-aware steering better preserves the intended belief family. Our work demonstrates an example of linear field probing (LFP) as a simple approach to tile the data manifold and make interventions that respect the underlying geometry. We conclude that rich structure emerges naturally in LLMs and that purely linear concept representations are often an inadequate abstraction.

papers.title: Identifying and Mitigating the Influence of the Prior Distribution in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does the implicit prior distribution in LLMs influence their responses on deterministic tasks, and can we identify interventions to mitigate this influence?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs encode information needed to solve prior-dominated tasks, and identifies two interventions—prompting and lightweight finetuning—that can mitigate the influence of the prior and improve performance.
papers.conclusion: LLMs encode the information necessary to solve prior-dominated tasks, and prompting and lightweight finetuning can reduce the influence of the prior, potentially reducing hallucinations related to prior probability.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting the model to not rely on prior knowledge improves performance on prior-dominated tasks.
The prior is encoded in specific layers of the model, as shown by logit lens analysis.
Lightweight finetuning (LoRA) with a stratified train-validation split significantly improves performance on prior-dominated tasks.
Finetuning is more effective for prior-dominated tasks than for prior-insensitive tasks.
After finetuning, model performance no longer correlates with prior probability but with task difficulty.
papers.limitation: The prior is encoded in LLMs in a complex way such that linear methods such as steering do not improve performance, and probing cannot test the model's understanding on a stratified validation setup.
future_direction: Future improvements in situations where LLMs hallucinate for reasons related to the prior probability of token sequences.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) sometimes fail to respond appropriately to deterministic tasks -- such as counting or forming acronyms -- because the implicit prior distribution they have learned over sequences of tokens influences their responses. In this work, we show that, in at least some cases, LLMs actually compute the information needed to perform these tasks correctly, and we identify some interventions that can allow them to access this information to improve their performance. First, we show that simply prompting the language model to not rely on its prior knowledge leads to dramatic improvements in prior-dominated tasks. We then use mechanistic interpretability techniques to localize the prior within the LLM and manipulate the extent to which that prior influences its responses. Specifically, we show that it is possible to identify layers of the underlying neural network that correlate with the prior probability of a response and that lightweight finetuning of these layers with basic prompts on prior-dominated tasks achieves high performance on held-out answers. These results suggest that the information required to produce a correct response is contained within the representations of the problems formed by the models. Furthermore, we show that this finetuning is significantly more effective for prior-dominated tasks, and that the error after finetuning is no longer correlated with the prior. Our results suggest that it may be possible to define effective methods for manipulating the extent to which LLMs rely upon their priors in solving problems, potentially increasing their performance in settings where LLMs hallucinate for reasons related to the prior probability of token sequences.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: Towards detecting unanticipated bias in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) and Explainable AI (XAI) methods be used to detect unanticipated biases in Large Language Models (LLMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes using post-hoc, model-agnostic Uncertainty Quantification and Explainable AI methods as novel avenues for detecting unanticipated biases in Large Language Models, aiming to make AI systems fairer and more transparent.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that Uncertainty Quantification and Explainable AI are promising techniques for detecting unanticipated biases in LLMs, contributing to the development of more transparent, accountable, and unbiased AI technologies, though significant challenges remain.
papers.key_findings:
Current bias research focuses on known biases (e.g., gender, race) and mitigation, leaving a gap in detecting subtle, unanticipated biases.
Uncertainty Quantification methods like Test-Time Data Augmentation, Ensemble Methods, and Verbal Uncertainty could reveal biases by analyzing variation in model outputs.
Explainable AI methods, particularly perturbation-based approaches, surrogate models, and prompting, can help users identify if protected attributes are unduly influencing model decisions.
A major challenge is the subjective nature of bias and fairness, and the difficulty of obtaining completely bias-free data for LLM training.
The proposed UQ and XAI approaches are post-hoc and model-agnostic, making them applicable to a wide range of LLMs, including proprietary ones.
papers.limitation:
Any data generated by humans holds the potential of carrying bias, making it impossible to obtain completely bias-free data and models.
The closed-source nature of many popular LLMs limits the ability to analyze models at a computational level or fine-tune them for higher bias sensitivity.
UQ and XAI results cannot be disentangled from other influences (e.g., model capability limits), and these methods may not uncover all socially unacceptable biases.
The proposed approaches cannot fully automatically detect biases; they only offer clues, leaving the final detection responsibility and its potential pitfalls (like human prejudice) to users.
future_direction: Exploring Uncertainty Quantification methods like Test-Time Data Augmentation, Ensemble Methods, and Verbal Uncertainty for bias detection.
Applying Explainable AI methods, particularly perturbation-based approaches and surrogate models, to uncover unanticipated biases.
Developing evaluation frameworks and visualization tools to help users interpret UQ and XAI results for bias detection in their specific tasks.
papers.abstract: Over the last year, Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT have become widely available and have exhibited fairness issues similar to those in previous machine learning systems. Current research is primarily focused on analyzing and quantifying these biases in training data and their impact on the decisions of these models, alongside developing mitigation strategies. This research largely targets well-known biases related to gender, race, ethnicity, and language. However, it is clear that LLMs are also affected by other, less obvious implicit biases. The complex and often opaque nature of these models makes detecting such biases challenging, yet this is crucial due to their potential negative impact in various applications. In this paper, we explore new avenues for detecting these unanticipated biases in LLMs, focusing specifically on Uncertainty Quantification and Explainable AI methods. These approaches aim to assess the certainty of model decisions and to make the internal decision-making processes of LLMs more transparent, thereby identifying and understanding biases that are not immediately apparent. Through this research, we aim to contribute to the development of fairer and more transparent AI systems.

papers.title: Probing Pretrained Language Models for Lexical Semantics
papers.research_question: How do different strategies for extracting lexical type-level knowledge from pretrained language models impact performance across languages and tasks? Is lexical knowledge concentrated in few parameters or scattered? How do these representations compare to traditional static word vectors? Do monolingual LMs learn similar representations for translation pairs?
papers.core_contribution: A systematic study of how to extract lexical type-level knowledge from pretrained language models, showing that lexical information is concentrated in lower layers and that extracted representations can outperform traditional static word embeddings in some tasks.
papers.conclusion: Pretrained language models store a wealth of type-level lexical knowledge, and effective extraction depends on configuration choices such as using monolingual LMs, averaging over lower layers, and excluding special tokens.
papers.key_findings:
Monolingual LMs contain more lexical information than multilingual LMs.
Lexical information is concentrated in lower Transformer layers.
Averaging over multiple layers (especially lower ones) yields better representations than single layers.
Excluding special tokens [CLS] and [SEP] improves performance.
Extracted representations can outperform fastText in monolingual tasks but underperform in cross-lingual tasks.
future_direction: Investigating how domains of external corpora affect AOC configurations and sampling representative contexts.
Extending the study to more languages, tasks, and larger underlying LMs.
Developing more sophisticated lexical representation extraction methods (e.g., layer weighting or attention).
papers.abstract: The success of large pretrained language models (LMs) such as BERT and RoBERTa has sparked interest in probing their representations, in order to unveil what types of knowledge they implicitly capture. While prior research focused on morphosyntactic, semantic, and world knowledge, it remains unclear to which extent LMs also derive lexical type-level knowledge from words in context. In this work, we present a systematic empirical analysis across six typologically diverse languages and five different lexical tasks, addressing the following questions: 1) How do different lexical knowledge extraction strategies (monolingual versus multilingual source LM, out-of-context versus in-context encoding, inclusion of special tokens, and layer-wise averaging) impact performance? How consistent are the observed effects across tasks and languages? 2) Is lexical knowledge stored in few parameters, or is it scattered throughout the network? 3) How do these representations fare against traditional static word vectors in lexical tasks? 4) Does the lexical information emerging from independently trained monolingual LMs display latent similarities? Our main results indicate patterns and best practices that hold universally, but also point to prominent variations across languages and tasks. Moreover, we validate the claim that lower Transformer layers carry more type-level lexical knowledge, but also show that this knowledge is distributed across multiple layers.

papers.title: Vision-Language Introspection: Mitigating Overconfident Hallucinations in MLLMs via Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering
papers.research_question: How to mitigate overconfident hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by simulating a metacognitive self-correction process that diagnoses and rectifies internal visual-semantic misalignments?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that mitigates object hallucinations in MLLMs by first introspectively localizing causal visual anchors and then performing interpretable bi-causal steering to rectify internal representations and calibrate overconfidence.
papers.conclusion: VLI effectively mitigates overconfident hallucinations in MLLMs by introspectively diagnosing visual-semantic conflicts and actively steering internal representations towards verified visual evidence, achieving state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
VLI reduces the object hallucination rate by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improves accuracy by up to 6.33% on POPE compared to baseline models.
Bi-causal steering, which isolates visual evidence from background noise via counterfactual representations, is the most critical component for error rectification.
The method successfully localizes interpretable visual anchors corresponding to high-risk tokens, enabling precise intervention.
VLI demonstrates robust generalization across diverse datasets (MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, GQA) and model architectures (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen3-VL).
Adaptive confidence calibration effectively penalizes ungrounded certainty, mitigating persistent hallucinations driven by blind confidence.
papers.limitation: The method introduces increased computational latency and memory overhead due to the parallel processing of counterfactual branches, though optimization reduces the impact.
papers.abstract: Object hallucination critically undermines the reliability of Multimodal Large Language Models, often stemming from a fundamental failure in cognitive introspection, where models blindly trust linguistic priors over specific visual evidence. Existing mitigations remain limited: contrastive decoding approaches operate superficially without rectifying internal semantic misalignments, while current latent steering methods rely on static vectors that lack instance-specific precision. We introduce Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that simulates a metacognitive self-correction process. VLI first performs Attributive Introspection to diagnose hallucination risks via probabilistic conflict detection and localize the causal visual anchors. It then employs Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering to actively modulate the inference process, dynamically isolating visual evidence from background noise while neutralizing blind confidence through adaptive calibration. VLI achieves state-of-the-art performance on advanced models, reducing object hallucination rates by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improving accuracy by 5.8% on POPE.

papers.title: Analysing the Residual Stream of Language Models Under Knowledge Conflicts
papers.research_question: Can we identify the conflict between context and parameter knowledge by probing the residual stream? Can we know which source of knowledge the models will use before they generate the answers?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally register knowledge conflict signals in the residual stream, which can be detected by probing intermediate activations. The residual stream shows distinct skewness patterns when the model relies on contextual versus parametric knowledge, enabling prediction of the model's knowledge selection behavior.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit internal mechanisms for identifying conflicts in the mid-layers, and the residual stream shows distinct skewness patterns when the model uses context and parametric knowledge to predict. This analysis provides insights into the behaviour of LLMs in the presence of knowledge conflicts.
papers.key_findings:
The signal of knowledge conflict rises from intermediate layers (e.g., layer 13-14) and can be detected with high accuracy using linear probing.
The residual stream exhibits different skewness patterns (measured by Kurtosis, Hoyer, Gini) when the model uses contextual knowledge versus parametric knowledge.
The decision of which knowledge to use occurs after the detection of the knowledge conflict signal.
The probing model's performance for conflict detection peaks around the 14th layer and then decreases slightly.
The skewness patterns are more pronounced in hidden states than in MLP or Self-Attention activations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can store a significant amount of factual knowledge in their parameters. However, their parametric knowledge may conflict with the information provided in the context. Such conflicts can lead to undesirable model behaviour, such as reliance on outdated or incorrect information. In this work, we investigate whether LLMs can identify knowledge conflicts and whether it is possible to know which source of knowledge the model will rely on by analysing the residual stream of the LLM. Through probing tasks, we find that LLMs can internally register the signal of knowledge conflict in the residual stream, which can be accurately detected by probing the intermediate model activations. This allows us to detect conflicts within the residual stream before generating the answers without modifying the input or model parameters. Moreover, we find that the residual stream shows significantly different patterns when the model relies on contextual knowledge versus parametric knowledge to resolve conflicts. This pattern can be employed to estimate the behaviour of LLMs when conflict happens and prevent unexpected answers before producing the answers. Our analysis offers insights into how LLMs internally manage knowledge conflicts and provides a foundation for developing methods to control the knowledge selection processes.

papers.title: Understanding Reasoning in Thinking Language Models via Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: Can reasoning behaviors in thinking language models be controlled using steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that reasoning behaviors in thinking LLMs are mediated by linear directions in the activation space and can be controlled using steering vectors extracted via difference of means and attribution patching.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors provide a practical method for controlling reasoning behaviors in thinking models, opening new possibilities for fine-grained control of model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Thinking models exhibit distinct reasoning behaviors such as backtracking, uncertainty estimation, and example testing.
These behaviors are mediated by linear directions in the model's activation space.
Steering vectors extracted via difference of means can control these behaviors, increasing or decreasing their occurrence.
The steering approach works across different model architectures within the DeepSeek-R1-Distill family.
The method provides a practical tool for modulating reasoning capabilities in thinking models.
papers.limitation:
The automated annotation process using GPT-4o has occasionally produced false positives and false negatives in identifying reasoning patterns.
The generalization of these findings to other models that have undergone reward-based RL training instead of being fine-tuned on thinking models remains an open question.
future_direction: Developing more robust annotation methods, potentially incorporating multiple models or human validation.
Extending the research to a broader range of models to understand the universality of thinking mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have led to the development of thinking language models that generate extensive internal reasoning chains before producing responses. While these models achieve improved performance, controlling their reasoning processes remains challenging. This work presents a steering approach for thinking LLMs by analyzing and manipulating specific reasoning behaviors in DeepSeek-R1-Distill models. Through a systematic experiment on 500 tasks across 10 diverse categories, we identify several reasoning behaviors exhibited by thinking models, including expressing uncertainty, generating examples for hypothesis validation, and backtracking in reasoning chains. We demonstrate that these behaviors are mediated by linear directions in the model's activation space and can be controlled using steering vectors. By extracting and applying these vectors, we provide a method to modulate specific aspects of the model's reasoning process, such as its tendency to backtrack or express uncertainty. Our approach offers practical tools for steering reasoning processes in thinking models in a controlled and interpretable manner. We validate our steering method using three DeepSeek-R1-Distill models, demonstrating consistent control across different model architectures.

papers.title: CLUE: Non-parametric Verification from Experience via Hidden-State Clustering
papers.abstract: Assessing the quality of Large Language Model (LLM) outputs presents a critical challenge. Previous methods either rely on text-level information (e.g., reward models, majority voting), which can overfit to superficial cues, or on calibrated confidence from token probabilities, which would fail on less-calibrated models. Yet both of these signals are, in fact, partial projections of a richer source of information: the model's internal hidden states. Early layers, closer to token embeddings, preserve semantic and lexical features that underpin text-based judgments, while later layers increasingly align with output logits, embedding confidence-related information. This paper explores hidden states directly as a unified foundation for verification. We show that the correctness of a solution is encoded as a geometrically separable signature within the trajectory of hidden activations. To validate this, we present Clue (Clustering and Experience-based Verification), a deliberately minimalist, non-parametric verifier. With no trainable parameters, CLUE only summarizes each reasoning trace by an hidden state delta and classifies correctness via nearest-centroid distance to ``success'' and ``failure'' clusters formed from past experience. The simplicity of this method highlights the strength of the underlying signal. Empirically, CLUE consistently outperforms LLM-as-a-judge baselines and matches or exceeds modern confidence-based methods in reranking candidates, improving both top-1 and majority-vote accuracy across AIME 24/25 and GPQA. As a highlight, on AIME 24 with a 1.5B model, CLUE boosts accuracy from 56.7% (majority@64) to 70.0% (top-maj@16).

papers.title: Can LLMs Predict Their Own Failures? Self-Awareness via Internal Circuits
papers.research_question: Can LLMs predict their own failures by inspecting internal states during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Gnosis, a lightweight self-awareness mechanism that enables frozen LLMs to perform intrinsic self-verification by decoding signals from hidden states and attention patterns with negligible inference overhead.
papers.conclusion: Gnosis provides a highly efficient framework for self-evaluation and sibling modeling, enabling early error detection and compute-aware control, demonstrating that intrinsic self-verification is both scalable and cost-effective.
papers.key_findings:
Gnosis consistently outperforms strong internal baselines and large external judges (e.g., 8B reward models, Gemini 2.5 Pro) in accuracy and calibration across math reasoning, QA, and academic knowledge benchmarks.
Gnosis generalizes zero-shot to partial generations, enabling early detection of failing trajectories and compute-aware control.
A Gnosis head trained on a small backbone transfers effectively to judge larger sibling models without fine-tuning.
Gnosis adds only ~5M parameters and operates with negligible inference cost, independent of sequence length.
Results show that reliable correctness cues are intrinsic to the generation process and can be extracted efficiently without external supervision.
papers.limitation: Gnosis is designed as a self-awareness mechanism rather than a general-purpose reward model; it transfers robustly to siblings but is not capable of acting as a general reward model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generate fluent and complex outputs but often fail to recognize their own mistakes and hallucinations. Existing approaches typically rely on external judges, multi-sample consistency, or text-based self-critique, which incur additional compute or correlate weakly with true correctness. We ask: can LLMs predict their own failures by inspecting internal states during inference? We introduce Gnosis, a lightweight self-awareness mechanism that enables frozen LLMs to perform intrinsic self-verification by decoding signals from hidden states and attention patterns. Gnosis passively observes internal traces, compresses them into fixed-budget descriptors, and predicts correctness with negligible inference cost, adding only ~5M parameters and operating independently of sequence length. Across math reasoning, open-domain question answering, and academic knowledge benchmarks, and over frozen backbones ranging from 1.7B to 20B parameters, Gnosis consistently outperforms strong internal baselines and large external judges in both accuracy and calibration. Moreover, it generalizes zero-shot to partial generations, enabling early detection of failing trajectories and compute-aware control. These results show that reliable correctness cues are intrinsic to generation process and can be extracted efficiently without external supervision.

papers.title: Truth-value judgment in language models: 'truth directions' are context sensitive
papers.research_question: How does context affect the truth-value probes in large language models, and are these probes coherently incorporating contextual information?
papers.core_contribution: Truth-value probes are context sensitive but also sensitive to irrelevant information, and truth-value directions causally mediate natural language inference.
papers.conclusion: Truth-value directions are context sensitive and causally mediate inference, but probes are not fully coherent.
papers.key_findings:
Truth-value probes are sensitive to context, but also to irrelevant information.
The type of errors (consistency errors) depend on the layer, model, and data.
Probes trained without premises (no-prem) still show context sensitivity, indicating that prior beliefs are not represented independently.
Instruction-tuned models show different error patterns (more E4 errors) compared to pretrained-only models.
Truth-value directions causally mediate natural language inference (intervention experiment).
papers.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that the latent spaces of large language models (LLMs) contain directions predictive of the truth of sentences. Multiple methods recover such directions and build probes that are described as uncovering a model's "knowledge" or "beliefs". We investigate this phenomenon, looking closely at the impact of context on the probes. Our experiments establish where in the LLM the probe's predictions are (most) sensitive to the presence of related sentences, and how to best characterize this kind of sensitivity. We do so by measuring different types of consistency errors that occur after probing an LLM whose inputs consist of hypotheses preceded by (negated) supporting and contradicting sentences. We also perform a causal intervention experiment, investigating whether moving the representation of a premise along these truth-value directions influences the position of an entailed or contradicted sentence along that same direction. We find that the probes we test are generally context sensitive, but that contexts which should not affect the truth often still impact the probe outputs. Our experiments show that the type of errors depend on the layer, the model, and the kind of data. Finally, our results suggest that truth-value directions are causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.

papers.title: ReflCtrl: Controlling LLM Reflection via Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: When does the model initiate reflection during its reasoning process? How does reflection influence the model's reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ReflCtrl, a representation engineering framework that extracts a reflection direction in the latent space to control self-reflection in reasoning LLMs, and shows that reflections are often redundant and can be reduced to save inference cost without sacrificing performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes ReflCtrl for controlling self-reflection in reasoning LLMs, demonstrates reflection redundancy and its connection to internal uncertainty, and shows that stepwise steering can reduce inference cost with minimal accuracy loss.
papers.key_findings:
Reflections are redundant, especially in stronger models, and up to 33.6% of reasoning tokens can be saved while preserving performance.
The model's reflection behavior is highly correlated with internal uncertainty signals, implying self-reflection may be controlled by model's uncertainty.
Stepwise steering can control reflection frequency and reduces performance loss compared to all-token steering.
The reflection direction can be used to predict answer correctness, suggesting it encodes uncertainty information.
Smaller models are more sensitive to reflection reduction than larger models.
papers.limitation:
Identification of reasoning steps relies on keyword search, which may be model specific.
ReflCtrl only works for open-source models and it remains unclear whether it generalizes to SOTA closed-source models such as GPT-4 or Claude.
future_direction: developing uncertainty-aware dynamic steering to adjust steering strength during inference
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning have achieved strong performance across diverse tasks, including mathematics, coding, and general reasoning. A distinctive ability of these reasoning models is self-reflection: the ability to review and revise previous reasoning steps. While self-reflection enhances reasoning performance, it also increases inference cost. In this work, we study self-reflection through the lens of representation engineering. We segment the model's reasoning into steps, identify the steps corresponding to reflection, and extract a reflection direction in the latent space that governs this behavior. Using this direction, we propose a stepwise steering method that can control reflection frequency. We call our framework ReflCtrl. Our experiments show that (1) in many cases reflections are redundant, especially in stronger models (in our experiments, we can save up to 33.6 percent of reasoning tokens while preserving performance), and (2) the model's reflection behavior is highly correlated with an internal uncertainty signal, implying self-reflection may be controlled by the model's uncertainty.

papers.title: LMEnt: A Suite for Analyzing Knowledge in Language Models from Pretraining Data to Representations
papers.research_question: How do language models acquire and represent knowledge from pretraining data, and what is the interplay between data composition, training dynamics, and internal knowledge mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LMEnt, a suite for analyzing knowledge acquisition in language models, including annotated pretraining data, entity-based retrieval, and pretrained models, enabling studies on the connection between data and knowledge representations.
papers.conclusion: LMEnt provides a flexible testbed for investigating knowledge representations in language models and facilitates future research on knowledge acquisition and editing.
papers.key_findings:
LMEnt's entity-based retrieval outperforms string-based methods by up to 80.4% in returning relevant document chunks.
LMEnt models achieve comparable knowledge recall performance to models trained on orders of magnitude more data.
Knowledge acquisition is correlated with fact frequency, but both learning and forgetting rates increase with frequency.
Increasing model size improves learning of frequent facts but has little effect on tail facts.
papers.limitation:
Pretraining data is relatively small and models are compute-efficient, which may limit generalizability.
Does not compare with dense retrievers like DPR or ColBERT.
Focuses only on pretraining, not mid- or post-training phases.
future_direction: Investigating knowledge plasticity and editing during pretraining.
Improving factuality of LMs using entity annotations.
Extending LMEnt to other data sources and architectures.
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) increasingly drive real-world applications that require world knowledge. However, the internal processes through which models turn data into representations of knowledge and beliefs about the world, are poorly understood. Insights into these processes could pave the way for developing LMs with knowledge representations that are more consistent, robust, and complete. To facilitate studying these questions, we present LMEnt, a suite for analyzing knowledge acquisition in LMs during pretraining. LMEnt introduces: (1) a knowledge-rich pretraining corpus, fully annotated with entity mentions, based on Wikipedia, (2) an entity-based retrieval method over pretraining data that outperforms previous approaches by as much as 80.4%, and (3) 12 pretrained models with up to 1B parameters and 4K intermediate checkpoints, with comparable performance to popular open-sourced models on knowledge benchmarks. Together, these resources provide a controlled environment for analyzing connections between entity mentions in pretraining and downstream performance, and the effects of causal interventions in pretraining data. We show the utility of LMEnt by studying knowledge acquisition across checkpoints, finding that fact frequency is key, but does not fully explain learning trends. We release LMEnt to support studies of knowledge in LMs, including knowledge representations, plasticity, editing, attribution, and learning dynamics.

papers.title: The Compositional Architecture of Regret in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Which transformer layers’ hidden states most cleanly isolate the regret signal, and how is this signal represented with these layers?
papers.core_contribution: This work contributes valuable insights for neuron-level identification and provides methodological tools for analyzing similar cognitive states, advancing our understanding of how cognitive states are coded within LLMs.
papers.conclusion: This work advances our understanding of how cognitive states like regret are coded within LLMs through neuron-level identification and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Identified the optimal regret representation layer using the S-CDI metric, enhancing probe classification performance.
Discovered an M-shaped decoupling pattern across transformer layers, indicating alternating coupling and decoupling phases in information processing.
Categorized neurons into three functional groups (regret, non-regret, dual) using the RDS metric.
Showed that simultaneous intervention with regret and dual neurons substantially reduces regret classification performance, revealing a compositional architecture of regret at the neuron level.
Revealed that regret processing capabilities exhibit non-monotonic scaling across model sizes, with the 70B model showing superior performance.
papers.limitation: The non-monotonic scaling observed lacks more detailed investigation.
future_direction: Validation of the two-factor performance hypothesis in future work.
papers.abstract: Regret in Large Language Models refers to their explicit regret expression when presented with evidence contradicting their previously generated misinformation. Studying the regret mechanism is crucial for enhancing model reliability and helps in revealing how cognition is coded in neural networks. To understand this mechanism, we need to first identify regret expressions in model outputs, then analyze their internal representation. This analysis requires examining the model's hidden states, where information processing occurs at the neuron level. However, this faces three key challenges: (1) the absence of specialized datasets capturing regret expressions, (2) the lack of metrics to find the optimal regret representation layer, and (3) the lack of metrics for identifying and analyzing regret neurons. Addressing these limitations, we propose: (1) a workflow for constructing a comprehensive regret dataset through strategically designed prompting scenarios, (2) the Supervised Compression-Decoupling Index (S-CDI) metric to identify optimal regret representation layers, and (3) the Regret Dominance Score (RDS) metric to identify regret neurons and the Group Impact Coefficient (GIC) to analyze activation patterns. Our experimental results successfully identified the optimal regret representation layer using the S-CDI metric, which significantly enhanced performance in probe classification experiments. Additionally, we discovered an M-shaped decoupling pattern across model layers, revealing how information processing alternates between coupling and decoupling phases. Through the RDS metric, we categorized neurons into three distinct functional groups: regret neurons, non-regret neurons, and dual neurons.

papers.title: Too Big to Fool: Resisting Deception in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models of varying capacities within the same family balance in-context information against their internal world models, particularly when faced with intentionally misleading prompts?
papers.core_contribution: Larger language models exhibit greater resilience to deceptive prompts, demonstrating an advanced ability to integrate conflicting in-context information with their internal knowledge, without simply ignoring prompts or relying on memorization.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces an evaluation strategy that re-uses existing benchmarks with minimal changes to study LLM behavior. Experiments show that larger models are more resilient to deceptive prompts, indicating a better ability to integrate prompt information with internal knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models consistently show a smaller Relative Accuracy Drop when given deceptive hints, indicating higher resilience to misinformation.
Larger models do not ignore in-context information; they effectively follow legitimate instructions and utilize truthful hints.
The resilience is not due to memorization, as shown by control experiments with overfitted models and a model without prior exposure to the test data.
Larger models generally exhibit better instruction-following capabilities, except for the Gemma family which is an outlier.
Models can infer missing information from answer choices, maintaining accuracy above chance even when the question is removed.
papers.limitation:
The study focused exclusively on multiple-choice datasets, which may not capture nuances of open-ended or generative tasks.
Experiments involved only open-source LLMs, limiting generalizability to proprietary models with different architectures or training.
papers.abstract: Large language models must balance their weight-encoded knowledge with in-context information from prompts to generate accurate responses. This paper investigates this interplay by analyzing how models of varying capacities within the same family handle intentionally misleading in-context information. Our experiments demonstrate that larger models exhibit higher resilience to deceptive prompts, showcasing an advanced ability to interpret and integrate prompt information with their internal knowledge. Furthermore, we find that larger models outperform smaller ones in following legitimate instructions, indicating that their resilience is not due to disregarding in-context information. We also show that this phenomenon is likely not a result of memorization but stems from the models' ability to better leverage implicit task-relevant information from the prompt alongside their internally stored knowledge.

papers.title: The wall confronting large language models
papers.research_question: How do scaling laws limit the ability of large language models to improve prediction uncertainty and reliability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the scaling laws of large language models severely limit their ability to improve prediction uncertainty, and proposes a theoretical explanation linking low scaling exponents to non-Gaussian fluctuations, error pileup, and a potential degenerative AI pathway.
papers.conclusion: The degenerative AI pathway is plausible given the scaling laws and theoretical mechanisms, but it can be avoided by prioritizing insight and understanding over brute-force scaling.
papers.key_findings:
Scaling exponents for LLMs are very low (around 0.1), leading to diminishing returns in error reduction with increased compute.
The trade-off between learning (generating non-Gaussian output distributions) and accuracy leads to error pileup and potential information catastrophes.
The Calude-Longo deluge of spurious correlations in large datasets exacerbates the problem by overwhelming true correlations.
The resilience of uncertainty (RoU) in non-Gaussian distributions requires exponentially more data to achieve the same accuracy as Gaussian processes.
Degenerative AI (DAI) is a plausible but avoidable pathway for LLMs if they continue to rely on brute-force scaling without insight.
papers.limitation: The theoretical analysis is based on simplified models and may not capture all complexities of real LLMs.
future_direction: Prioritize insight and understanding over brute-force scaling.
Use the scientific method to distinguish true correlations from spurious ones in data.
papers.abstract: We show that the scaling laws which determine the performance of large language models (LLMs) severely limit their ability to improve the uncertainty of their predictions. As a result, raising their reliability to meet the standards of scientific inquiry is intractable by any reasonable measure. We argue that the very mechanism which fuels much of the learning power of LLMs, namely the ability to generate non-Gaussian output distributions from Gaussian input ones, might well be at the roots of their propensity to produce error pileup, ensuing information catastrophes and degenerative AI behaviour. This tension between learning and accuracy is a likely candidate mechanism underlying the observed low values of the scaling components. It is substantially compounded by the deluge of spurious correlations pointed out by Calude and Longo which rapidly increase in any data set merely as a function of its size, regardless of its nature. The fact that a degenerative AI pathway is a very probable feature of the LLM landscape does not mean that it must inevitably arise in all future AI research. Its avoidance, which we also discuss in this paper, necessitates putting a much higher premium on insight and understanding of the structural characteristics of the problems being investigated.

papers.title: Getting a CLUE: A Method for Explaining Uncertainty Estimates
papers.research_question: How can we interpret uncertainty estimates from probabilistic models by finding counterfactual explanations that indicate how to change an input to make the model more confident?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Counterfactual Latent Uncertainty Explanations (CLUE), a method to generate counterfactual explanations for uncertainty estimates by searching in the latent space of a deep generative model, and proposes a framework for evaluating such explanations.
papers.conclusion: CLUE is an effective method for generating counterfactual explanations of uncertainty, outperforming baselines and helping practitioners understand sources of uncertainty.
papers.key_findings:
CLUE outperforms baseline methods in explaining uncertainty across multiple datasets.
CLUE generates counterfactuals that are on the data manifold and plausible.
The proposed computational evaluation framework allows for quantitative assessment of counterfactual explanations.
User studies demonstrate that CLUE helps practitioners predict on which new inputs a BNN will be uncertain.
papers.limitation:
CLUE relies on the quality of the auxiliary deep generative model; if the DGM fails to capture the data manifold, CLUE may generate unrealistic counterfactuals.
CLUE is designed for differentiable probabilistic models, which may limit its applicability.
future_direction: Extending CLUE to other types of uncertainty estimates.
Exploring the use of CLUE in active learning and Bayesian optimization.
Investigating other distance metrics for the counterfactual search.
papers.abstract: Both uncertainty estimation and interpretability are important factors for trustworthy machine learning systems. However, there is little work at the intersection of these two areas. We address this gap by proposing a novel method for interpreting uncertainty estimates from differentiable probabilistic models, like Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). Our method, Counterfactual Latent Uncertainty Explanations (CLUE), indicates how to change an input, while keeping it on the data manifold, such that a BNN becomes more confident about the input's prediction. We validate CLUE through 1) a novel framework for evaluating counterfactual explanations of uncertainty, 2) a series of ablation experiments, and 3) a user study. Our experiments show that CLUE outperforms baselines and enables practitioners to better understand which input patterns are responsible for predictive uncertainty.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Knowledge from Quirky Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we elicit latent knowledge from language models that are finetuned to make systematic errors, using probes on their activations?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on middle-layer activations can extract context-independent knowledge from language models finetuned to output untruthfully, enabling elicitation of correct answers despite deceptive outputs.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that context-independent representations of knowledge exist in quirky models, and probing methods can reliably extract truth, informing scalable oversight of capable systems.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on truthful contexts generalize to untruthful contexts, indicating context-independent knowledge representations.
The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 75% of the performance gap between truthful and untruthful behavior on hard examples.
Mechanistic anomaly detection using Mahalanobis distance can flag untruthful behavior with an average AUROC of 0.95.
Difference-in-means probing directions are more causally implicated in model output and show better robustness to distribution shifts.
Unsupervised methods like CCS and CRC have an inductive bias towards context-independent generalization but achieve lower in-distribution performance.
papers.limitation:
Measurement of difficulty is a significant limitation, as different difficulty metrics are minimally correlated.
Contrast pair activations come from the answer token position, which is out-of-distribution for the finetuning data.
future_direction: Expand on the diversity and representativeness of evaluations by constructing new quirky datasets and models.
Investigate the limits of context-independent representations by varying the number of personas in finetuning.
Characterize the causal mechanisms involved, such as how intervening on knowledge representations affects output.
papers.abstract: Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK) aims to find patterns in a capable neural network's activations that robustly track the true state of the world, especially in hard-to-verify cases where the model's output is untrusted. To further ELK research, we introduce 12 datasets and a corresponding suite of "quirky" language models (LMs) that are finetuned to make systematic errors when answering questions if and only if the keyword "Bob" is present in the prompt. We find that, especially in middle layers, linear probes usually report an LM's knowledge independently of what the LM outputs, enabling us to elicit the correct answer despite the model's untruthful output. The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 89% of the gap in AUROC between truthful and untruthful contexts, and 75% for questions harder than those used to train the probe. We also find that a mechanistic anomaly detection approach can flag untruthful behavior with 0.95 AUROC. Our results show promise for eliciting reliable knowledge from capable but untrusted models, and facilitates future research empirically investigating ELK methods.

papers.title: Believe It or Not: How Deeply do LLMs Believe Implanted Facts?
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether LLMs genuinely believe facts implanted via knowledge editing techniques, and develops a framework to measure the depth of such beliefs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework to measure belief depth in LLMs for implanted facts, operationalized through generality, robustness, and internal representations. It finds that Synthetic Document Finetuning (SDF) often implants beliefs deeply, while prompting and mechanistic editing fail.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that measuring belief depth is crucial for evaluating knowledge editing, and while SDF can implant deep beliefs, its effectiveness varies with fact plausibility.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting and mechanistic editing fail to implant knowledge deeply; beliefs are not robust and have internal representations distinct from genuine knowledge.
Synthetic Document Finetuning (SDF) often succeeds in implanting beliefs that generalize to related contexts, are robust to scrutiny, and have similar internal representations to genuine knowledge.
SDF's success depends on fact plausibility; implanted beliefs that contradict basic world knowledge are brittle and representationally distinct.
Implanted beliefs from SDF are robust to increased inference-time compute, with minimal impact on belief rates.
Internal representations of SDF-implanted facts resemble genuine knowledge for plausible facts, but adversarial probes can distinguish implausible ones.
papers.limitation: SDF's success is not universal; implanted beliefs that contradict basic world knowledge are brittle and representationally distinct.
future_direction: Continued evaluation of SDF on highly capable future systems
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing techniques promise to implant new factual knowledge into large language models (LLMs). But do LLMs really believe these facts? We develop a framework to measure belief depth and use it to evaluate the success of knowledge editing techniques. We operationalize belief depth as the extent to which implanted knowledge 1) generalizes to related contexts (e.g. Fermi estimates several logical steps removed), 2) is robust to self-scrutiny and direct challenge, and 3) is represented similarly to genuine knowledge (as measured by linear probes). Our evaluations show that simple prompting and mechanistic editing techniques fail to implant knowledge deeply. In contrast, Synthetic Document Finetuning (SDF) - where models are trained on LLM-generated documents consistent with a fact - often succeeds at implanting beliefs that behave similarly to genuine knowledge. However, SDF's success is not universal, as implanted beliefs that contradict basic world knowledge are brittle and representationally distinct from genuine knowledge. Overall, our work introduces measurable criteria for belief depth and enables the rigorous evaluation necessary for deploying knowledge editing in real-world applications.

papers.title: Truth is Universal: Robust Detection of Lies in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we robustly detect when Large Language Models (LLMs) are lying by analyzing their internal activations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a universal two-dimensional subspace in LLM activations containing a general truth direction (tG) and a polarity-sensitive direction (tP), which explains prior generalization failures and enables the construction of a robust lie detector (TTPD).
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates a universal two-dimensional internal representation of truth in LLMs, clarifies prior generalization failures, and provides a robust method (TTPD) for lie detection, advancing towards general-purpose, transparent, and safe AI.
papers.key_findings:
A two-dimensional subspace in the residual stream activations separates true and false statements, containing a general truth direction (tG) and a polarity-sensitive direction (tP).
The affirmative truth direction (tA) from prior work is a linear combination of tG and tP, explaining its failure to generalize to negated statements.
The two-dimensional truth representation is universal across multiple LLM families and sizes (e.g., LLaMA, Gemma, Mistral).
The proposed TTPD method, which uses the tG direction, achieves state-of-the-art accuracy (94%) in detecting lies in both simple factual statements and complex real-world scenarios.
The truth subspace remains two-dimensional even when considering more complex statement types (logical conjunctions/disjunctions) and different languages (German).
papers.limitation:
TTPD uses only one of the two dimensions (tG) of the truth subspace; a non-linear classifier using both tG and tP might achieve higher accuracy.
The generalization of TTPD is tested on a limited number of statement types and real-world scenarios.
The analysis only shows the truth subspace is at least two-dimensional; examining more statement types might reveal additional linear or non-linear structures.
The findings' applicability to larger LLMs or multimodal models is not tested.
future_direction: Explore a non-linear classifier using both tG and tP for higher accuracy.
Test generalization across a broader range of statement types and diverse real-world contexts.
Study the effects of interventions on the 2D truth subspace during inference on model outputs.
Determine whether the findings apply to larger LLMs or multimodal models.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionised natural language processing, exhibiting impressive human-like capabilities. In particular, LLMs are capable of "lying", knowingly outputting false statements. Hence, it is of interest and importance to develop methods to detect when LLMs lie.
