Indeed, several authors trained classifiers to detect LLM lies based on their internal model activations. However, other researchers showed that these classifiers may fail to generalise, for example to negated statements. In this work, we aim to develop a robust method to detect when an LLM is lying. To this end, we make the following key contributions: (i) We demonstrate the existence of a two-dimensional subspace, along which the activation vectors of true and false statements can be separated. Notably, this finding is universal and holds for various LLMs, including Gemma-7B, LLaMA2-13B, Mistral-7B and LLaMA3-8B. Our analysis explains the generalisation failures observed in previous studies and sets the stage for more robust lie detection; (ii) Building upon (i), we construct an accurate LLM lie detector. Empirically, our proposed classifier achieves state-of-the-art performance, attaining 94% accuracy in both distinguishing true from false factual statements and detecting lies generated in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: Influential Training Data Retrieval for Explaining Verbalized Confidence of LLMs
papers.research_question: What drives confidence in LLMs, and do they ground their confidence in content-related training examples or superficial confidence-related cues?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TracVC, a method for tracing verbalized confidence in LLMs back to training data, and finds that LLMs often rely on superficial confidence cues rather than content grounding.
papers.conclusion: TracVC reveals that LLMs are often influenced by confidence-related training data, indicating a limitation in current training regimes. The method provides a data-centric approach for improving trustworthiness in confidence expression.
papers.key_findings:
OLMo2-13B is frequently influenced by confidence-related training data that is lexically unrelated to the query, suggesting it mimics linguistic expressions of certainty.
Larger LLMs do not demonstrate higher content groundness than smaller ones, possibly due to higher sensitivity to stylistic patterns.
Content groundness is higher when tested on samples that are correctly answered by the LLM.
Post-training techniques can impact content groundness in opposite directions on different LLMs.
LLMs may learn to sound confident without understanding when confidence is justified, highlighting a limitation in training regimes.
papers.limitation:
Constrained to a limited set of LLMs, primarily OLMo and Llama families, due to data availability.
Simplified separation of content- and confidence-related influences, which may overlap in practice.
Limited coverage due to retrieval-based approach and fixed number of retrieved examples.
Use of TracIn for influence estimation, without comparison to alternative methods like Hessian-based approaches.
future_direction: Future research on how pre-training and fine-tuning strategies shape confidence grounding.
Extending TracVC to study other aspects of model behavior like answer selection and reasoning patterns.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can increase users' perceived trust by verbalizing confidence in their outputs. However, prior work has shown that LLMs are often overconfident, making their stated confidence unreliable since it does not consistently align with factual accuracy. To better understand the sources of this verbalized confidence, we introduce TracVC (\textbf{Trac}ing \textbf{V}erbalized \textbf{C}onfidence), a method that builds on information retrieval and influence estimation to trace generated confidence expressions back to the training data. We evaluate TracVC on OLMo and Llama models in a question answering setting, proposing a new metric, content groundness, which measures the extent to which an LLM grounds its confidence in content-related training examples (relevant to the question and answer) versus in generic examples of confidence verbalization. Our analysis reveals that OLMo2-13B is frequently influenced by confidence-related data that is lexically unrelated to the query, suggesting that it may mimic superficial linguistic expressions of certainty rather than rely on genuine content grounding. These findings point to a fundamental limitation in current training regimes: LLMs may learn how to sound confident without learning when confidence is justified. Our analysis provides a foundation for improving LLMs' trustworthiness in expressing more reliable confidence.

papers.title: LLM Internal States Reveal Hallucination Risk Faced With a Query
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs can estimate their own hallucination risk before response generation using internal states.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLM internal states can indicate whether a query was seen in training data and predict hallucination risk, achieving high accuracy with a probing estimator.
papers.conclusion: This work demonstrates that LLMs have latent self-assessment capabilities to estimate hallucination risks prior to response generation.
papers.key_findings:
Internal states can distinguish seen/unseen queries with 80.28% accuracy.
Internal states can estimate hallucination risk with 84.32% accuracy across 15 NLG tasks.
Layer depth positively correlates with prediction performance.
Internal states are model-specific but allow some zero-shot transfer.
Features in internal states are shared within tasks but not across tasks.
papers.limitation:
Lack of human evaluation in data labeling process.
Trade-off in performance compared to methods using both query and response.
papers.abstract: The hallucination problem of Large Language Models (LLMs) significantly limits their reliability and trustworthiness. Humans have a self-awareness process that allows us to recognize what we don't know when faced with queries. Inspired by this, our paper investigates whether LLMs can estimate their own hallucination risk before response generation. We analyze the internal mechanisms of LLMs broadly both in terms of training data sources and across 15 diverse Natural Language Generation (NLG) tasks, spanning over 700 datasets. Our empirical analysis reveals two key insights: (1) LLM internal states indicate whether they have seen the query in training data or not; and (2) LLM internal states show they are likely to hallucinate or not regarding the query. Our study explores particular neurons, activation layers, and tokens that play a crucial role in the LLM perception of uncertainty and hallucination risk. By a probing estimator, we leverage LLM self-assessment, achieving an average hallucination estimation accuracy of 84.32\% at run time.

papers.title: Patchscopes: A Unifying Framework for Inspecting Hidden Representations of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we leverage the model itself to explain its internal representations in natural language, and how can a configurable patching framework be used to decode information from hidden representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Patchscopes, a modular framework for decoding information from hidden representations in LLMs, which unifies prior interpretability methods and enables more expressive, robust, and training-data-free inspection.
papers.conclusion: Patchscopes provides a unifying framework for inspecting hidden representations that mitigates shortcomings of prior methods and opens up new possibilities for more expressive and robust interpretation, including practical benefits like correcting multi-hop reasoning errors.
papers.key_findings:
Patchscopes outperforms vocabulary projection methods (Logit Lens, Tuned Lens) in decoding next-token predictions from intermediate layers across multiple models.
Patchscopes can extract specific attributes from hidden representations without training data, outperforming linear probes in 6 out of 12 commonsense and factual reasoning tasks.
Patchscopes can verbalize the gradual entity resolution process in early layers, where vocabulary projections fail.
Patchscopes enables cross-model inspection, allowing a more capable model to explain representations of a smaller model.
Patchscopes can correct latent multi-hop reasoning errors, achieving 50% accuracy on a complex task, outperforming chain-of-thought and vanilla generation.
papers.limitation:
The framework only reveals if specific information can be decoded from the patched representation via the post-patching computation, but does not guarantee the representation stores all that information.
The method may suffer from placeholder contamination where the placeholder token in the target prompt interferes with the generation.
future_direction: Quantify qualitative observations of entity resolution and placeholder contamination.
Study to what extent placeholder contamination can be mitigated with a different placeholder choice.
Investigate why some models might be more susceptible to placeholder contamination than others.
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal representations of large language models (LLMs) can help explain models' behavior and verify their alignment with human values. Given the capabilities of LLMs in generating human-understandable text, we propose leveraging the model itself to explain its internal representations in natural language. We introduce a framework called Patchscopes and show how it can be used to answer a wide range of questions about an LLM's computation. We show that many prior interpretability methods based on projecting representations into the vocabulary space and intervening on the LLM computation can be viewed as instances of this framework. Moreover, several of their shortcomings such as failure in inspecting early layers or lack of expressivity can be mitigated by Patchscopes. Beyond unifying prior inspection techniques, Patchscopes also opens up new possibilities such as using a more capable model to explain the representations of a smaller model, and multihop reasoning error correction.

papers.title: Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models trained on English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual transformers like Llama-2 use English as an internal pivot language, with intermediate layers representing concepts in English before mapping to the target language, indicating an English bias in their internal representations.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual LLMs have an English bias in their internal representations, which may lead to linguistic biases and has implications for equitable AI.
papers.key_findings:
In translation tasks, intermediate layers decode the English version of the correct next token before switching to the target language.
The forward pass goes through three phases: input space, concept space (biased towards English), and output space.
Token energy is low in middle layers, indicating that latents are in a concept space orthogonal to token space.
The English bias is less pronounced for languages with single-token words (like Chinese) in repetition tasks.
The same pattern is observed in Mistral-7B, suggesting generality of the phenomenon.
papers.limitation:
Focus on Llama-2 family, so claims may not generalize to other models.
Tasks are simple and controlled, not real-world.
Limited understanding of the concept space structure.
Logit lens only reveals part of the internal state.
future_direction: Investigate how English bias affects downstream model behavior.
Study how English bias changes with different training data or tokenizers.
Extend to a wider range of tasks and models.

papers.title: Don't Make It Up: Preserving Ignorance Awareness in LLM Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: How can we fine-tune LLMs to incorporate new knowledge without eroding their aligned epistemic abstention behavior (the ability to acknowledge when the model does not know)?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SEAT, a fine-tuning method that combines sparse updates and entity-perturbed regularization to preserve a model's epistemic abstention (ability to say 'I don't know') while adapting it to new knowledge, without requiring alignment data or post-hoc re-alignment.
papers.conclusion: SEAT is an effective method for preserving epistemic abstention during knowledge adaptation, establishing preservation of abstention as a useful objective for safer model adaptation.
papers.key_findings:
SEAT preserves epistemic abstention on unseen queries (improving human-evaluated abstention by 18%–101% over baselines) while maintaining near-perfect target knowledge acquisition.
Both sparse training and entity-perturbed regularization are essential for SEAT's strong performance; ablations show each component alone is insufficient.
SEAT constrains activation drift on unseen data, keeping representations anchored near the base model's, while allowing meaningful shifts for fine-tuning data.
SEAT outperforms a range of baselines including full fine-tuning, LoRA, EWC, CLoRA, R-tuning, and experience replay in preserving abstention behavior.
SEAT preserves downstream utility across a diverse range of tasks (e.g., truthfulness, QA, reasoning) compared to the base model.
papers.limitation:
The optimal sparsity ratio needs to be tuned to balance learning efficacy and abstention preservation.
The method is empirically grounded and does not provide formal guarantees.
papers.abstract: Existing work on mitigating catastrophic forgetting during large language models (LLMs) fine-tuning for new knowledge instances has primarily focused on preserving performance on previously seen data, while critically overlooking the collapse of essential capabilities instilled through alignment, most notably the model's ability to faithfully express epistemic uncertainty (a property we term 'Ignorance Awareness'). In this work, we formalize the notion of Ignorance Awareness and illustrate that conventional fine-tuning methods can result in substantial activation displacement. This displacement undermines the critical capability of ignorance awareness, leading to undesirable behaviors such as hallucinations. To address this challenge, we introduce SEAT, a simple and principled fine-tuning approach that not only enables the model to effectively acquire new knowledge instances but also preserves its aligned ignorance awareness. SEAT integrates two key components: (1) sparse tuning that constrains activation drift, and (2) a novel entity perturbation method designed to counter knowledge entanglement. Experimental results demonstrate that, across both real-world and synthetic datasets, SEAT significantly outperforms baselines in preserving ignorance awareness while retaining optimal fine-tuning performance, offering a more robust solution for LLM fine-tuning.

papers.title: Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens (CORAL): Transferrable and Calibration-Aware Inference-Time Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve both accuracy and calibration of LLMs during inference by directly steering using correctness signals from internal activations, rather than optimizing proxies?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CORAL, a lightweight inference-time steering method that uses regularized MLP probes on residual activations to improve accuracy and calibration in MCQA tasks, with demonstrated transferability across benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CORAL provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference by extracting distributed correctness signals via regularized probes.
papers.key_findings:
CORAL consistently improves accuracy and calibration across three 7B models and multiple MCQA benchmarks.
CORAL's learned steering directions transfer without retraining to four held-out benchmarks, averaging 14% accuracy and 49% ECE improvements.
Correctness signals are distributed across many neurons and require supervised aggregation; sparse methods like SAE fail to capture them.
Middle layers (17-21) contain the most useful correctness signals for steering.
Regularized probes capture distributed correctness signals that sparse methods miss.
papers.limitation:
Limited to multiple-choice question answering; generalization to free-form generation is open.
Requires labeled data to train probes, which may not be available for all domains or languages.
Adds inference latency due to activation extraction and probe prediction.
Transfer performance depends on similarity between source and target tasks; dissimilar tasks yield smaller improvements.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit persistent miscalibration, especially after instruction tuning and preference alignment. Modified training objectives can improve calibration, but retraining is expensive. Inference-time steering offers a lightweight alternative, yet most existing methods optimize proxies for correctness rather than correctness itself. We introduce CORAL (Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens), a regularized inference-time steering method that captures distributed correctness signals from model internal activations using weight-decay MLP probes. We evaluate CORAL across three 7B-parameter models and find that it consistently improves accuracy by 10\% and expected calibration error (ECE) by 50\% on average. We additionally demonstrate that these gains transfer without retraining to the complete published test sets of four held-out benchmarks (ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, Math-MC, OpenBookQA), averaging 14\% accuracy improvements and 49\% ECE improvements. Our results support the hypothesis that distributed information in model internals can be extracted using regularized probes when individual neurons are insufficient. CORAL thus provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference.

papers.title: Learning Inductive Biases with Simple Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do simple neural networks develop inductive biases like the shape bias, and under what conditions? How does the acquisition of this bias relate to vocabulary acceleration, mirroring child development?
papers.core_contribution: Simple neural networks can learn a shape bias from very few examples, and the development of this bias predicts vocabulary acceleration in the networks, consistent with developmental processes in children.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can learn inductive biases like the shape bias from limited data, and the dynamics of this learning mirror child development, suggesting a connection between artificial and human learning.
papers.key_findings:
Multilayer perceptrons develop a shape bias after seeing as few as 3 examples of 4 object categories using abstract bit-vector patterns.
Convolutional neural networks develop a shape bias with as few as 6 examples of 8 object categories using synthetic images.
Networks show greater sensitivity to changes in shape than color after shape bias training, as shown by parametric manipulation of stimuli.
The development of the shape bias in CNNs correlates with the onset of vocabulary acceleration, mirroring the correlation observed in children.
Color bias training requires less data than shape bias training and does not follow the same two-step generalization process.
future_direction: Investigate the hypothesis of initializing large-scale image recognition models with shape bias training using ImageNet-scale DNNs.
papers.abstract: People use rich prior knowledge about the world in order to efficiently learn new concepts. These priors - also known as "inductive biases" - pertain to the space of internal models considered by a learner, and they help the learner make inferences that go beyond the observed data. A recent study found that deep neural networks optimized for object recognition develop the shape bias (Ritter et al., 2017), an inductive bias possessed by children that plays an important role in early word learning. However, these networks use unrealistically large quantities of training data, and the conditions required for these biases to develop are not well understood. Moreover, it is unclear how the learning dynamics of these networks relate to developmental processes in childhood. We investigate the development and influence of the shape bias in neural networks using controlled datasets of abstract patterns and synthetic images, allowing us to systematically vary the quantity and form of the experience provided to the learning algorithms. We find that simple neural networks develop a shape bias after seeing as few as 3 examples of 4 object categories. The development of these biases predicts the onset of vocabulary acceleration in our networks, consistent with the developmental process in children.

papers.title: Uncertainty and interpretability in convolutional neural networks for semantic segmentation of colorectal polyps
papers.research_question: How can recent advances in uncertainty estimation and interpretability be incorporated into Fully Convolutional Networks for polyp segmentation, and what performance improvements do they yield?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that enhancing Fully Convolutional Networks with batch normalization, transfer learning, and incorporating Monte Carlo Dropout for uncertainty estimation and Guided Backpropagation for interpretability leads to improved performance in polyp segmentation and provides insights into model predictions.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that CNNs are effective for polyp segmentation, and incorporating uncertainty modeling and interpretability techniques enhances their trustworthiness and applicability in medical settings.
papers.key_findings:
EFCN-8 achieves a mean IoU of 76.06%, outperforming previous state-of-the-art methods.
Inclusion of batch normalization and transfer learning significantly improves segmentation accuracy.
ESegNet, with fewer parameters, achieves comparable results to FCN-8 but is outperformed by EFCN-8 when enhanced.
Uncertainty estimation via Monte Carlo Dropout reveals high uncertainty at polyp borders and in false positive regions.
Guided Backpropagation visualizations show that models rely on edge information for polyp segmentation.
papers.limitation: The results of uncertainty and interpretability methods are open to interpretation and lack a theoretical framework for analysis.
future_direction: Exploring recent architectures for semantic segmentation
Applying Relevance Propagation for increased interpretability
Incorporating Conditional Random Fields for improved spatial coherence
papers.abstract: Colorectal polyps are known to be potential precursors to colorectal cancer, which is one of the leading causes of cancer-related deaths on a global scale. Early detection and prevention of colorectal cancer is primarily enabled through manual screenings, where the intestines of a patient is visually examined. Such a procedure can be challenging and exhausting for the person performing the screening. This has resulted in numerous studies on designing automatic systems aimed at supporting physicians during the examination. Recently, such automatic systems have seen a significant improvement as a result of an increasing amount of publicly available colorectal imagery and advances in deep learning research for object image recognition. Specifically, decision support systems based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance on both detection and segmentation of colorectal polyps. However, CNN-based models need to not only be precise in order to be helpful in a medical context. In addition, interpretability and uncertainty in predictions must be well understood. In this paper, we develop and evaluate recent advances in uncertainty estimation and model interpretability in the context of semantic segmentation of polyps from colonoscopy images. Furthermore, we propose a novel method for estimating the uncertainty associated with important features in the input and demonstrate how interpretability and uncertainty can be modeled in DSSs for semantic segmentation of colorectal polyps. Results indicate that deep models are utilizing the shape and edge information of polyps to make their prediction. Moreover, inaccurate predictions show a higher degree of uncertainty compared to precise predictions.

papers.title: Beyond the Rosetta Stone: Unification Forces in Generalization Dynamics
papers.research_question: What causes cross-lingual factual errors in language models, and how can we understand and improve cross-lingual transfer?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a controlled 'Petri dish' methodology to study cross-lingual knowledge transfer dynamics, identifies a crucial early phase where models develop unified or separate representations across languages, and shows that unification predicts cross-lingual generalization.
papers.conclusion: Controlled settings can shed light on pre-training dynamics and suggest new directions for improving cross-lingual transfer in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Models undergo an early learning phase where they develop either unified or separate representations for the same facts across languages.
Unification of representations is essential for cross-lingual factual transfer.
The degree of unification depends on the mutual information between facts and training data language, and on how easy it is to extract the language feature.
Cross-lingual transfer can be improved without increasing parallel data by manipulating data distribution and tokenization to reduce the language feature's representational footprint.
A unification score, measuring similarity of representations across languages, strongly predicts cross-lingual factual recall accuracy.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) struggle with cross-lingual knowledge transfer: they hallucinate when asked in one language about facts expressed in a different language during training. This work introduces a controlled setting to study the causes and dynamics of this phenomenon by training small Transformer models from scratch on synthetic multilingual datasets. We identify a learning phase wherein a model develops either separate or unified representations of the same facts across languages, and show that unification is essential for cross-lingual transfer. We also show that the degree of unification depends on mutual information between facts and training data language, and on how easy it is to extract that language. Based on these insights, we develop methods to modulate the level of cross-lingual transfer by manipulating data distribution and tokenization, and we introduce metrics and visualizations to formally characterize their effects on unification. Our work shows how controlled settings can shed light on pre-training dynamics and suggests new directions for improving cross-lingual transfer in LLMs.

papers.title: Uncovering Uncertainty in Transformer Inference
papers.research_question: How do transformer models iteratively refine predictions during inference, and can cross-entropy-based metrics detect uncertainty in token generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides empirical support for the Iterative Inference Hypothesis in transformers and introduces a cross-entropy-based method to detect uncertainty during token generation, showing distinct differences between correct and incorrect outputs.
papers.conclusion: The paper supports the Iterative Inference Hypothesis and demonstrates that cross-entropy-based metrics can detect uncertainty in transformer token generation, with potential for flagging hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
The nth token embedding in the residual stream follows a trajectory of decreasing loss, supporting the Iterative Inference Hypothesis.
Cross-entropy between residual predictions and target distributions shows observable differences between correct and incorrect generations.
Output cross-entropy with respect to the sampled token is a strong predictor of correctness on the idiom dataset, with an AUC of 0.92.
Cross-entropy metrics capture uncertainty in open-ended generations, with spikes corresponding to erroneous or uncertain tokens.
papers.limitation: The cross-entropy measure captures both prompt-inherent and model uncertainty, and cannot disambiguate between them; it also fails for confidently incorrect models.
future_direction: Expanding analysis to a broad range of datasets and language models of varying sizes.
Extending the study to multi-token generations.
Exploring additional convergence metrics for predicting correct versus incorrect generations.
papers.abstract: We explore the Iterative Inference Hypothesis (IIH) within the context of transformer-based language models, aiming to understand how a model's latent representations are progressively refined and whether observable differences are present between correct and incorrect generations. Our findings provide empirical support for the IIH, showing that the nth token embedding in the residual stream follows a trajectory of decreasing loss. Additionally, we observe that the rate at which residual embeddings converge to a stable output representation reflects uncertainty in the token generation process. Finally, we introduce a method utilizing cross-entropy to detect this uncertainty and demonstrate its potential to distinguish between correct and incorrect token generations on a dataset of idioms.

papers.title: Linear Spatial World Models Emerge in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models implicitly encode linear spatial world models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides empirical evidence that large language models encode linear spatial world models, showing that spatial relations are represented in a low-dimensional subspace with geometric structure and are functionally used by the model.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that large language models do encode a basic spatial world model linearly within their representations.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes achieve near-perfect accuracy in decoding spatial relations, indicating linear encoding.
PCA reveals a low-dimensional subspace where spatial relations are organized geometrically (inverse relations are antipodal, orthogonal relations are perpendicular).
Spatial representations are compositional: composed relations correspond to vector sums of atomic relations.
Object positions are consistently represented in the same spatial subspace.
Causal interventions (activation steering) show that the spatial subspace is functionally used by the model for prediction.
papers.limitation:
The work does not investigate other essential components of a full world model, such as temporal dynamics or object permanence.
The analysis focuses on a limited set of spatial relations.
The generality of the findings to other model types remains an open question.
future_direction: Extending the framework to cover a broader and more diverse set of spatial directions.
Investigating other components of world models such as temporal dynamics.
Testing generalization to other model types.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated emergent abilities across diverse tasks, raising the question of whether they acquire internal world models. In this work, we investigate whether LLMs implicitly encode linear spatial world models, which we define as linear representations of physical space and object configurations. We introduce a formal framework for spatial world models and assess whether such structure emerges in contextual embeddings. Using a synthetic dataset of object positions, we train probes to decode object positions and evaluate geometric consistency of the underlying space. We further conduct causal interventions to test whether these spatial representations are functionally used by the model. Our results provide empirical evidence that LLMs encode linear spatial world models.

papers.title: Circuit Stability Characterizes Language Model Generalization
papers.research_question: Can circuit stability characterize and predict generalization in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit stability as a method to assess model performance and shows it can characterize and predict different aspects of generalization.
papers.conclusion: Circuit stability characterizes generalization in language models and provides an actionable way to assess and improve model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit stability predicts length, structural, and compositional generalization in arithmetic reasoning tasks.
Circuit instability in arithmetic indicates lack of understanding of commutativity and associativity.
For Boolean expression evaluation, circuit non-equivalence indicates structural generalization issues.
Chain-of-thought prompting induces circuit stability and improves performance.
Circuit stability is a robust estimator of model performance that can be computed efficiently.
papers.limitation:
Empirical case studies are limited in terms of tasks and models.
Computational cost of circuit discovery can be high for very large models.
Constructing partitions manually requires prior knowledge of the task.
future_direction: Extending circuit stability to other modalities and architectures.
Investigating the connection between circuit stability and generalization bounds.
Automating the construction of partitions for complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Extensively evaluating the capabilities of (large) language models is difficult. Rapid development of state-of-the-art models induce benchmark saturation, while creating more challenging datasets is labor-intensive. Inspired by the recent developments in mechanistic interpretability, we introduce circuit stability as a new way to assess model performance. Circuit stability refers to a model's ability to apply a consistent reasoning process-its circuit-across various inputs. We mathematically formalize circuit stability and circuit equivalence. Then, through three case studies, we empirically show that circuit stability and the lack thereof can characterize and predict different aspects of generalization. Our proposed methods offer a step towards rigorously relating the generality of models to their interpretability.

papers.title: Characterizing Truthfulness in Large Language Model Generations with Local Intrinsic Dimension
papers.research_question: How can we characterize and predict the truthfulness of LLM-generated texts using the local intrinsic dimension of model activations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes using the local intrinsic dimension (LID) of internal activations to detect hallucinations in LLM outputs, demonstrating improved performance over uncertainty-based methods and providing insights into model behavior through LID analysis.
papers.conclusion: Proposes using local intrinsic dimension (LID) to characterize and predict LLM output truthfulness, achieving better performance than prior methods and opening a new direction for quantifying model truthfulness.
papers.key_findings:
LID-based methods (LID-MLE and LID-GeoMLE) outperform entropy-based and verbalized uncertainty methods in detecting hallucinations across multiple QA datasets.
The intrinsic dimension of representations exhibits a 'hunchback' shape across layers: increasing in early layers and decreasing in later layers.
The intrinsic dimension of truthful answers is consistently lower than untruthful answers across token positions, with a sharp decrease near the end for truthful answers.
Instruction tuning increases the intrinsic dimension of representations, and intrinsic dimension correlates with generalization performance during tuning.
LID methods are robust to cross-task reference and hyperparameter choices, maintaining effectiveness even with out-of-distribution neighbors.
papers.limitation:
The paper mainly discusses LLM generations in English, so results may be biased towards the English-speaking population.
The paper focuses primarily on question-answering scenarios.
future_direction: Implement the LID method on diverse tasks and languages, as well as cross-lingual settings.
Further investigate the 'shifting behind' phenomenon between LID values and detection performance across layers.
papers.abstract: We study how to characterize and predict the truthfulness of texts generated from large language models (LLMs), which serves as a crucial step in building trust between humans and LLMs. Although several approaches based on entropy or verbalized uncertainty have been proposed to calibrate model predictions, these methods are often intractable, sensitive to hyperparameters, and less reliable when applied in generative tasks with LLMs. In this paper, we suggest investigating internal activations and quantifying LLM's truthfulness using the local intrinsic dimension (LID) of model activations. Through experiments on four question answering (QA) datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness ohttps://info.arxiv.org/help/prep#abstractsf our proposed method. Additionally, we study intrinsic dimensions in LLMs and their relations with model layers, autoregressive language modeling, and the training of LLMs, revealing that intrinsic dimensions can be a powerful approach to understanding LLMs.

papers.title: Crawling The Internal Knowledge-Base of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we extract a structured knowledge graph representing the factual knowledge encoded in a language model, starting from a single seed entity?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a prompt-based method (LMCRAWL) to crawl a knowledge graph from a language model by decomposing the task into relation generation, object generation, and paraphrasing sub-tasks, achieving high precision.
papers.conclusion: The work presents a feasible method for extracting structured knowledge graphs from language models, representing an important step towards making the internal knowledge of LMs interpretable and usable.
papers.key_findings:
The LMCRAWL method achieves high precision (82-92%) in extracting factual triplets from GPT-3.
The number of facts extracted correlates with entity frequency in Wikidata, suggesting the model encodes more knowledge about popular entities.
Using a 'Don't Know' mechanism and paraphrasing improves precision and recall control.
The method can generate facts outside predefined schemas (e.g., Wikidata).
Automatic evaluation via Google search is a conservative estimate, with manual analysis suggesting true precision may be higher.
papers.limitation:
Cost and scalability issues limit the extraction of larger graphs (more hops).
Error propagation can occur when mistakes in early nodes lead to more mistakes in subsequent expansions.
Automatic precision evaluation is approximate and may underestimate true precision.
It is challenging to measure recall or knowledge coverage accurately.
The source of inaccuracies (extraction method vs. model knowledge) is not addressed.
future_direction: Expanding to larger graphs with more hops.
Introducing consistency constraints to increase precision.
Using the extracted knowledge graph as a question-answering mechanism.
papers.abstract: Language models are trained on large volumes of text, and as a result their parameters might contain a significant body of factual knowledge. Any downstream task performed by these models implicitly builds on these facts, and thus it is highly desirable to have means for representing this body of knowledge in an interpretable way. However, there is currently no mechanism for such a representation.Here, we propose to address this goal by extracting a knowledge-graph of facts from a given language model. We describe a procedure for "crawling" the internal knowledge-base of a language model. Specifically, given a seed entity, we expand a knowledge-graph around it. The crawling procedure is decomposed into sub-tasks, realized through specially designed prompts that control for both precision (i.e., that no wrong facts are generated) and recall (i.e., the number of facts generated). We evaluate our approach on graphs crawled starting from dozens of seed entities, and show it yields high precision graphs (82-92%), while emitting a reasonable number of facts per entity.

papers.title: Birds have four legs?! NumerSense: Probing Numerical Commonsense Knowledge of Pre-trained Language Models
papers.research_question: Does and to what extent do pre-trained language models capture numerical commonsense knowledge, and how robust is this knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a probing task and dataset (NumerSense) to evaluate numerical commonsense knowledge in pre-trained language models, finding that models perform poorly and are brittle to adversarial perturbations.
papers.conclusion: Powerful pre-trained models such as BERT and RoBERTa perform surprisingly poorly on numerical commonsense knowledge even after fine-tuning, and the introduced dataset provides a basis for future improvement.
papers.key_findings:
BERT and RoBERTa perform poorly on numerical commonsense knowledge without fine-tuning.
Fine-tuning with distant supervision improves performance but still far from human performance.
Models are brittle to adversarial examples (e.g., inserting adjectives).
Attention analysis shows that important words for numerical commonsense (subject/object) receive low attention weights.
Open-domain QA models also perform poorly on 'how-many' questions derived from NumerSense.
future_direction: Improving PTLMs' abilities to faithfully capture (numerical) commonsense.
Populating numerical facts in current commonsense knowledge bases.
Improving open-domain QA for 'how-many' questions.
Incorporating more structured inductive biases (e.g., dependencies and semantic roles) in pre-training.
Controlling bias in masked language modeling.
papers.abstract: Recent works show that pre-trained language models (PTLMs), such as BERT, possess certain commonsense and factual knowledge. They suggest that it is promising to use PTLMs as "neural knowledge bases" via predicting masked words. Surprisingly, we find that this may not work for numerical commonsense knowledge (e.g., a bird usually has two legs). In this paper, we investigate whether and to what extent we can induce numerical commonsense knowledge from PTLMs as well as the robustness of this process. To study this, we introduce a novel probing task with a diagnostic dataset, NumerSense, containing 13.6k masked-word-prediction probes (10.5k for fine-tuning and 3.1k for testing). Our analysis reveals that: (1) BERT and its stronger variant RoBERTa perform poorly on the diagnostic dataset prior to any fine-tuning; (2) fine-tuning with distant supervision brings some improvement; (3) the best supervised model still performs poorly as compared to human performance (54.06% vs 96.3% in accuracy).

papers.title: REACT: Representation Extraction And Controllable Tuning to Overcome Overfitting in LLM Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: How to overcome overfitting in LLM knowledge editing by precisely and controllably editing knowledge without overfitting to the edit target.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REACT, a two-phase framework for knowledge editing that extracts a belief-shift vector and applies controllable perturbations to hidden states, reducing overfitting while maintaining balanced editing performance.
papers.conclusion: REACT provides a practical framework for controlled knowledge editing, reducing overfitting and generalizing well, and points towards refining LLM editing without heavy parameter tuning.
papers.key_findings:
REACT achieves balanced performance across reliability, locality, and generality, outperforming baselines by at least 20 percentage points on average.
REACT shows high portability, indicating robust knowledge editing and resilience against overfitting.
REACT significantly reduces overfitting, as evidenced by lower Direct Probability scores and high Editing Overfit Scores on EVOKE.
REACT exhibits balanced calibration in Correct Answer Probability, avoiding overconfident updates.
REACT generalizes well across benchmarks, despite being trained only on COUNTERFACT.
papers.limitation:
Achieving the best possible performance typically requires fine-tuning or retraining on the specific dataset relevant to the task.
Further investigation is required to understand how edits influence broader linguistic abilities, including nuanced semantic understanding and language generation coherence.
papers.abstract: Large language model editing methods frequently suffer from overfitting, wherein factual updates can propagate beyond their intended scope, overemphasizing the edited target even when it's contextually inappropriate. To address this challenge, we introduce REACT (Representation Extraction And Controllable Tuning), a unified two-phase framework designed for precise and controllable knowledge editing. In the initial phase, we utilize tailored stimuli to extract latent factual representations and apply Principal Component Analysis with a simple learnbale linear transformation to compute a directional "belief shift" vector for each instance. In the second phase, we apply controllable perturbations to hidden states using the obtained vector with a magnitude scalar, gated by a pre-trained classifier that permits edits only when contextually necessary. Relevant experiments on EVOKE benchmarks demonstrate that REACT significantly reduces overfitting across nearly all evaluation metrics, and experiments on COUNTERFACT and MQuAKE shows that our method preserves balanced basic editing performance (reliability, locality, and generality) under diverse editing scenarios.

papers.title: Probing Language Models on Their Knowledge Source
papers.research_question: How do LLMs prioritize between their learned parametric knowledge (PK) and external contextual knowledge (CK) when faced with conflicting information?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a probing framework to study how LLMs select between parametric and contextual knowledge, showing that specific activations, especially from mid-layers and relation tokens, correlate with the knowledge source used.
papers.conclusion: Specific model activations correlate with knowledge source selection, and the probing framework generalizes across relation groups, enabling future work on controlling knowledge source behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Specific model activations are indicative of the knowledge source employed, with mid-layer activations, particularly those related to relations in the input, being crucial for prediction.
The most predictive features for knowledge source selection are those of the relation token in the query.
The knowledge source can be detected directly from the perturbing object token early in the inference process.
MHSA activations are less connected to the used knowledge source than MLP-L2 and MLP-L1 activations.
The probing framework successfully transfers learned knowledge source patterns from one relation group to another, demonstrating generalization.
papers.limitation:
The framework is designed to probe LLMs by introducing contradictions to their learned knowledge and does not account for situations where the knowledge remains unperturbed.
The study primarily measures correlation between activations and knowledge source use, but does not establish an explanation of the underlying process.
The framework uses a conventional subject-relation-object prompt structure, which may introduce biases; exploring alternative prompt structures could yield further insights.
future_direction: Extend the framework to handle cases where both parametric knowledge and contextual knowledge are consistent or not related.
Uncover the underlying mechanisms that govern knowledge source selection in LLMs through experimental designs that manipulate specific model parameters or activations.
Employ a variety of prompt structures to mitigate biases associated with the conventional subject-relation-object format.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often encounter conflicts between their learned, internal (parametric knowledge, PK) and external knowledge provided during inference (contextual knowledge, CK). Understanding how LLMs models prioritize one knowledge source over the other remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose a novel probing framework to explore the mechanisms governing the selection between PK and CK in LLMs. Using controlled prompts designed to contradict the model's PK, we demonstrate that specific model activations are indicative of the knowledge source employed. We evaluate this framework on various LLMs of different sizes and demonstrate that mid-layer activations, particularly those related to relations in the input, are crucial in predicting knowledge source selection, paving the way for more reliable models capable of handling knowledge conflicts effectively.

papers.title: Does Localization Inform Editing? Surprising Differences in Causality-Based Localization vs. Knowledge Editing in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does localization (specifically Causal Tracing) inform model editing? The paper investigates the relationship between where factual information is localized in a model and the success of editing that knowledge.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that localization results from Causal Tracing are essentially uncorrelated with the success of model editing methods like ROME and MEMIT, suggesting that mechanistic understanding of where knowledge is stored does not indicate the best place to edit it.
papers.conclusion: Counterintuitively, better mechanistic understanding of how pretrained language models store factual information (via Causal Tracing) does not translate to insights about which model layers to edit in order to best change their behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Model edit success (e.g., Rewrite Score) is statistically uncorrelated with where factual information is stored as measured by Causal Tracing.
The choice of which model layer to edit is a far better predictor of editing performance than the tracing effect at that layer.
This disconnect holds across multiple editing problem variants (Error Injection, Fact Erasure, Fact Amplification, Fact Forcing) and editing methods (ROME, MEMIT, constrained finetuning).
The finding generalizes across different causal localization methods (Causal Tracing, representation zeroing), editing metrics, models (GPT-J, GPT2-XL), and datasets (CounterFact, ZSRE).
Even for the editing problem variant most similar to Causal Tracing (Fact Forcing), tracing effects explain only a small fraction of variance in edit success compared to the edit layer choice.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to a particular set of localization and editing methods, including representation denoising/zeroing at the layer level and layer-level MLP editing methods. Conclusions may not hold for the breadth of localization and editing methods.
papers.abstract: Language models learn a great quantity of factual information during pretraining, and recent work localizes this information to specific model weights like mid-layer MLP weights. In this paper, we find that we can change how a fact is stored in a model by editing weights that are in a different location than where existing methods suggest that the fact is stored. This is surprising because we would expect that localizing facts to specific model parameters would tell us where to manipulate knowledge in models, and this assumption has motivated past work on model editing methods. Specifically, we show that localization conclusions from representation denoising (also known as Causal Tracing) do not provide any insight into which model MLP layer would be best to edit in order to override an existing stored fact with a new one. This finding raises questions about how past work relies on Causal Tracing to select which model layers to edit. Next, we consider several variants of the editing problem, including erasing and amplifying facts. For one of our editing problems, editing performance does relate to localization results from representation denoising, but we find that which layer we edit is a far better predictor of performance. Our results suggest, counterintuitively, that better mechanistic understanding of how pretrained language models work may not always translate to insights about how to best change their behavior. Our code is available at https://github.com/google/belief-localization

papers.title: How Do Large Language Models Acquire Factual Knowledge During Pretraining?
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge acquired during LLM pretraining, and how are LLMs affected by the training data at each step? How do training conditions affect the effectivity of factual knowledge acquisition? How is acquired factual knowledge forgotten, and how does training conditions affect forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes the dynamics of factual knowledge acquisition during LLM pretraining, revealing that acquisition occurs by accumulating small probability increases with each encounter, but is diluted by subsequent forgetting. It also finds that effectivity does not improve with more pretraining data, but model size helps, and forgetting follows a power-law.
papers.conclusion: Factual knowledge acquisition in LLM pretraining is a process of incremental probability increases countered by forgetting, and this understanding can explain phenomena like poor long-tail knowledge performance and the benefits of deduplication.
papers.key_findings:
Factual knowledge acquisition occurs by accumulating micro-acquisitions (small increases in log probability) with subsequent forgetting each time the model encounters the knowledge during pretraining.
Effectivity (immediate improvement in log probability) does not improve with more pretraining tokens, but does improve with larger model size.
Forgetting of acquired factual knowledge follows a power-law relationship with training steps (or tokens).
Training with duplicated data leads to faster forgetting compared to paraphrased data, highlighting the importance of deduplication.
Training with larger batch sizes makes models more robust to forgetting, enhancing knowledge acquisition.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent observation that large language models (LLMs) can store substantial factual knowledge, there is a limited understanding of the mechanisms of how they acquire factual knowledge through pretraining. This work addresses this gap by studying how LLMs acquire factual knowledge during pretraining. The findings reveal several important insights into the dynamics of factual knowledge acquisition during pretraining. First, counterintuitively, we observe that pretraining on more data shows no significant improvement in the model's capability to acquire and maintain factual knowledge. Next, there is a power-law relationship between training steps and forgetting of memorization and generalization of factual knowledge, and LLMs trained with duplicated training data exhibit faster forgetting. Third, training LLMs with larger batch sizes can enhance the models' robustness to forgetting. Overall, our observations suggest that factual knowledge acquisition in LLM pretraining occurs by progressively increasing the probability of factual knowledge presented in the pretraining data at each step. However, this increase is diluted by subsequent forgetting. Based on this interpretation, we demonstrate that we can provide plausible explanations for recently observed behaviors of LLMs, such as the poor performance of LLMs on long-tail knowledge and the benefits of deduplicating the pretraining corpus.

papers.title: Tracing the Roots of Facts in Multilingual Language Models: Independent, Shared, and Transferred Knowledge
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how factual knowledge is acquired and represented in multilingual language models, examining performance differences across languages, shared vs. independent representations, and mechanisms of cross-lingual transfer.
papers.core_contribution: This paper identifies three patterns of fact representation in multilingual language models—language-independent, cross-lingual shared, and cross-lingual transferred—and reveals limited effectiveness of cross-lingual knowledge transfer.
papers.conclusion: The study highlights the challenges in achieving effective cross-lingual transfer of factual knowledge and underscores the need for better representation learning and probing datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Factual probing performance varies across languages with moderate correlation to training data volume.
ML-LMs exhibit both language-independent and cross-lingual fact representations based on neuron activity patterns.
Cross-lingual knowledge transfer is limited and often localized to geographically proximate languages.
Easy-to-predict facts include shared entity tokens and naming cues, reducing apparent cross-lingual transfer.
Active neurons for facts in low-resource languages are more distributed in shallow layers compared to high-resource languages.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to encoder-based models (mBERT and XLM-R), and findings may not generalize to decoder-based models like BLOOM.
future_direction: Enhance cross-lingual fact representation learning in ML-LMs.
Develop a more precise factual probing dataset.
papers.abstract: Acquiring factual knowledge for language models (LMs) in low-resource languages poses a serious challenge, thus resorting to cross-lingual transfer in multilingual LMs (ML-LMs). In this study, we ask how ML-LMs acquire and represent factual knowledge. Using the multilingual factual knowledge probing dataset, mLAMA, we first conducted a neuron investigation of ML-LMs (specifically, multilingual BERT). We then traced the roots of facts back to the knowledge source (Wikipedia) to identify the ways in which ML-LMs acquire specific facts. We finally identified three patterns of acquiring and representing facts in ML-LMs: language-independent, cross-lingual shared and transferred, and devised methods for differentiating them. Our findings highlight the challenge of maintaining consistent factual knowledge across languages, underscoring the need for better fact representation learning in ML-LMs.

papers.title: Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition
papers.research_question: How can we steer language models by adding contrastive activation vectors to the residual stream, and how effective is this method?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), a method for steering language models by adding contrastive activation vectors to the residual stream, which effectively steers behavior, works on top of finetuning and system prompts, and minimally reduces capabilities.
papers.conclusion: CAA is an effective method for steering LLMs, providing precise control over behavior with minimal performance degradation, and offers insights into the linear representations of abstract concepts in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
CAA can effectively steer Llama 2 Chat models on a variety of alignment-relevant behaviors (AI Coordination, Corrigibility, Hallucination, Myopic Reward, Survival Instinct, Sycophancy, Refusal).
CAA generalizes from multiple-choice to open-ended generation tasks.
CAA can be combined with system prompting and finetuning to further control behavior.
CAA has minimal impact on general capabilities as measured by MMLU.
The steering vectors correspond intuitively to the presence of the behavior in the generated tokens (as shown by cosine similarity).
papers.limitation:
GPT-4 evaluation has limitations (sensitivity to prompt wording, biases).
Finetuning baseline was not fully optimized (hyperparameters, loss function).
Prompting baseline may not be fully optimized.
Vector normalization choices (norms vary across layers and behaviors).
future_direction: Steering at targeted token positions (instead of all tokens after the prompt).
Steering outside the residual stream (e.g., after MLP).
Application to red-teaming (using CAA to trigger unwanted behaviors).
papers.abstract: Nina Rimsky, Nick Gabrieli, Julian Schulz, Meg Tong, Evan Hubinger, Alexander Turner. Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

papers.title: Teaching Large Language Models to Express Knowledge Boundary from Their Own Signals
papers.research_question: How can we teach large language models to recognize and express their knowledge boundary, thereby reducing hallucinations caused by fabricating answers when they lack knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes COKE, an unsupervised method that leverages internal model signals (e.g., token probabilities) and multi-prompt consistency regularization to teach LLMs to express their knowledge boundaries, reducing hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: COKE effectively teaches LLMs to use their own internal signals to express knowledge boundaries, thereby reducing hallucinations by having the model admit ignorance when it lacks knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
The minimum token probability (Min-Prob) signal best reflects model confidence for knowledge boundary detection.
COKE enables models to express knowledge boundaries, significantly improving performance on in-domain and out-of-domain datasets compared to baseline methods.
Models trained with COKE learn to use internal confidence signals to decide when to answer or decline, generalizing better than supervised fine-tuning (IDK-FT) on out-of-domain data.
Consistency loss improves the model's generalization and ensures consistent knowledge boundary expression across different prompt types (prior, direct, posterior awareness).
The model's expression of 'Unknow' increases as its internal confidence score decreases, indicating it has learned to use the signal.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation divides test sets based on ground truth, ignoring the impact of the model's erroneous beliefs.
Focuses on short-form answers, not investigating long-form generation.
Does not extend to scenarios with external knowledge (e.g., RAG) or reasoning abilities (e.g., mathematics).
future_direction: Seeking more internal signals that better reflect the model's confidence and exploring how to combine these signals.
Extending the method to long-form generation and reasoning scenarios.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved great success, but their occasional content fabrication, or hallucination, limits their practical application. Hallucination arises because LLMs struggle to admit ignorance due to inadequate training on knowledge boundaries. We call it a limitation of LLMs that they can not accurately express their knowledge boundary, answering questions they know while admitting ignorance to questions they do not know. In this paper, we aim to teach LLMs to recognize and express their knowledge boundary, so they can reduce hallucinations caused by fabricating when they do not know. We propose CoKE, which first probes LLMs' knowledge boundary via internal confidence given a set of questions, and then leverages the probing results to elicit the expression of the knowledge boundary. Extensive experiments show CoKE helps LLMs express knowledge boundaries, answering known questions while declining unknown ones, significantly improving in-domain and out-of-domain performance.

papers.title: ReFT: Representation Finetuning for Language Models
papers.research_question: Can editing representations, instead of weights, be a more powerful alternative for parameter-efficient finetuning of language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Representation Finetuning (ReFT), a family of parameter-efficient finetuning methods that edit hidden representations instead of weights, and shows that it is more parameter-efficient and often outperforms existing PEFTs.
papers.conclusion: ReFT methods are a promising alternative to weight-based PEFTs, offering a better balance of efficiency and performance, and are worthy of further exploration.
papers.key_findings:
ReFT methods are 15×–65× more parameter-efficient than LoRA.
LoReFT achieves state-of-the-art performance on commonsense reasoning, instruction-following, and natural language understanding.
ReFT methods are less effective on arithmetic reasoning tasks, possibly due to the length of chain-of-thought generations.
ReFT performance scales with model size.
LoReFT outperforms full finetuning on instruction-following with only 0.0039% of parameters.
papers.limitation: ReFTs may have trouble with chain-of-thought reasoning tasks due to the length of generations and overall greater difficulty of the task.
papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods seek to adapt large neural models via updates to a small number of weights. However, much prior interpretability work has shown that representations encode rich semantic information, suggesting that editing representations might be a more powerful alternative. We pursue this hypothesis by developing a family of Representation Finetuning (ReFT) methods. ReFT methods operate on a frozen base model and learn task-specific interventions on hidden representations. We define a strong instance of the ReFT family, Low-rank Linear Subspace ReFT (LoReFT), and we identify an ablation of this method that trades some performance for increased efficiency. Both are drop-in replacements for existing PEFTs and learn interventions that are 15x--65x more parameter-efficient than LoRA. We showcase LoReFT on eight commonsense reasoning tasks, four arithmetic reasoning tasks, instruction-tuning, and GLUE. In all these evaluations, our ReFTs deliver the best balance of efficiency and performance, and almost always outperform state-of-the-art PEFTs. We release a generic ReFT training library publicly at https://github.com/stanfordnlp/pyreft.

papers.title: Unsupervised Real-Time Hallucination Detection based on the Internal States of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can hallucinations in large language models be detected in real-time using the models' internal states, without requiring manual annotations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MIND, an unsupervised framework for real-time hallucination detection using the internal states of LLMs, and HELM, a new benchmark for evaluating hallucination detection across multiple LLMs.
papers.conclusion: MIND is an effective unsupervised method for real-time hallucination detection, and the HELM benchmark facilitates future research in this area.
papers.key_findings:
MIND outperforms existing hallucination detection methods in terms of AUC and correlation.
MIND is highly efficient, taking only about 3% of the LLM's response generation time for detection.
Customized training data generated by the same LLM significantly improves hallucination detection performance.
The method is broadly effective across a variety of LLMs.
Using the contextualized embedding of the last token of the last layer is effective for hallucination detection.
papers.limitation: Detecting hallucinations using only the internal states of LLMs may not be as accurate as combining internal states with generated text.
future_direction: Integrating internal states of LLMs with generated text for improved hallucination detection.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in large language models (LLMs) refer to the phenomenon of LLMs producing responses that are coherent yet factually inaccurate. This issue undermines the effectiveness of LLMs in practical applications, necessitating research into detecting and mitigating hallucinations of LLMs. Previous studies have mainly concentrated on post-processing techniques for hallucination detection, which tend to be computationally intensive and limited in effectiveness due to their separation from the LLM's inference process. To overcome these limitations, we introduce MIND, an unsupervised training framework that leverages the internal states of LLMs for real-time hallucination detection without requiring manual annotations. Additionally, we present HELM, a new benchmark for evaluating hallucination detection across multiple LLMs, featuring diverse LLM outputs and the internal states of LLMs during their inference process. Our experiments demonstrate that MIND outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in hallucination detection.

papers.title: SeaKR: Self-aware Knowledge Retrieval for Adaptive Retrieval Augmented Generation
papers.research_question: How can we leverage the self-aware uncertainty from LLMs' internal states to dynamically determine when to retrieve and effectively integrate retrieved knowledge in adaptive RAG?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SEAKR, a novel adaptive RAG model that uses self-aware uncertainty extracted from LLMs' internal states (FFN layers) to dynamically decide when to retrieve and how to integrate retrieved knowledge, improving performance over existing adaptive RAG methods.
papers.conclusion: SEAKR is an effective adaptive RAG method that leverages self-aware uncertainty from LLMs' internal states to dynamically determine when to retrieve and how to integrate retrieved knowledge, outperforming existing adaptive baselines on QA tasks.
papers.key_findings:
SEAKR outperforms existing adaptive RAG methods on complex QA benchmarks (2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA, IIRC).
Self-aware re-ranking and self-aware reasoning are crucial components, with re-ranking providing more performance gain than self-aware retrieval alone.
SEAKR is effective on simple QA tasks but the performance gap compared to baselines is less pronounced than on complex QA.
SEAKR is a tuning-free method that generalizes well across different QA tasks without requiring fine-tuning.
The self-aware uncertainty estimator based on the Gram determinant of hidden representations effectively identifies when the LLM lacks knowledge.
papers.limitation:
Requires access to internal states of LLMs, limiting usability to open-sourced models.
Evaluated mainly on short-form question answering tasks, not on a broad spectrum of NLP tasks.
Computationally costly due to requiring 20 pseudo-generations for uncertainty estimation, though mitigated by parallel inference with vLLM.
Only tested on models up to 8 billion parameters due to limited computational resources.
Self-aware re-ranking may be surpassed by future advances in information retrieval technology.
future_direction: Explore new ways to estimate self-aware uncertainty from model outputs rather than internal states to apply to closed-source LLMs.
Evaluate SEAKR on a broader spectrum of natural language processing tasks, such as long-form QA and creative writing.
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Self-aware Knowledge Retrieval (SeaKR), a novel adaptive RAG model that extracts self-aware uncertainty of LLMs from their internal states. SeaKR activates retrieval when the LLMs present high self-aware uncertainty for generation. To effectively integrate retrieved knowledge snippets, SeaKR re-ranks them based on LLM's self-aware uncertainty to preserve the snippet that reduces their uncertainty to the utmost. To facilitate solving complex tasks that require multiple retrievals, SeaKR utilizes their self-aware uncertainty to choose among different reasoning strategies. Our experiments on both complex and simple Question Answering datasets show that SeaKR outperforms existing adaptive RAG methods. We release our code at https://github.com/THU-KEG/SeaKR.

papers.title: Filtering Beats Fine Tuning: A Bayesian Kalman View of In Context Learning in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can inference-time adaptation in large language models be interpreted as online Bayesian state estimation, and what are the theoretical properties of this formulation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a theory-first framework that interprets inference-time adaptation in LLMs as Bayesian filtering in a low-dimensional latent adaptation space, showing that rapid adaptation is driven by covariance collapse and that gradient-based methods arise as a singular limit of this probabilistic process.
papers.conclusion: The Bayesian filtering framework provides a principled, uncertainty-aware foundation for understanding inference-time learning in LLMs, with explicit guarantees on stability and information accumulation that are absent from optimization-based accounts.
papers.key_findings:
Inference-time learning in LLMs can be modeled as Bayesian filtering, where a latent adaptation state is sequentially inferred from token-level observations.
Covariance collapse—the rapid contraction of posterior uncertainty induced by informative tokens—precedes and drives convergence of the posterior mean, explaining few-shot generalization.
Gradient descent, natural-gradient methods, and meta-learning updates arise as singular, noise-free limits of the Bayesian filtering dynamics.
The framework provides explicit stability and sample efficiency guarantees based on observability conditions on token-level Jacobians.
This formulation unifies in-context learning, parameter-efficient adaptation, and test-time learning under a single probabilistic model with explicit uncertainty dynamics.
papers.limitation:
The analysis relies on local linearization and Gaussian noise assumptions, which may not fully capture the nonlinear structure of deep transformers.
Maintaining even structured covariance approximations may be computationally costly at scale.
future_direction: Extending the theory to nonlinear observation models and richer uncertainty representations.
Developing scalable approximations for large-scale foundation models.
Empirical validation in large-scale foundation models.
papers.abstract: We present a theory-first framework that interprets inference-time adaptation in large language models (LLMs) as online Bayesian state estimation. Rather than modeling rapid adaptation as implicit optimization or meta-learning, we formulate task- and context-specific learning as the sequential inference of a low-dimensional latent adaptation state governed by a linearized state-space model. Under Gaussian assumptions, adaptation follows a Kalman recursion with closed-form updates for both the posterior mean and covariance. This perspective elevates epistemic uncertainty to an explicit dynamical variable. We show that inference-time learning is driven by covariance collapse, i.e., rapid contraction of posterior uncertainty induced by informative tokens, which typically precedes convergence of the posterior mean. Using observability conditions on token-level Jacobians, we establish stability of the Bayesian filter, prove exponential covariance contraction rates, and derive mean-square error bounds. Gradient descent, natural-gradient methods, and meta-learning updates arise as singular, noise-free limits of the filtering dynamics, positioning optimization-based adaptation as a degenerate approximation of Bayesian inference. The resulting theory provides a unified probabilistic account of in-context learning, parameter-efficient adaptation, and test-time learning without parameter updates. It yields explicit guarantees on stability and sample efficiency, offers a principled interpretation of prompt informativeness via information accumulation, and clarifies the role of uncertainty dynamics absent from existing accounts. Minimal illustrative experiments corroborate the qualitative predictions of the theory.

papers.title: Decoding In-Context Learning: Neuroscience-inspired Analysis of Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context learning, and how do these changes mediate improvement in behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired framework using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Attention Ratio Analysis (ARA) to show that in-context learning improves task-critical representations and attention allocation, which correlate with behavioral gains.
papers.conclusion: ICL improves task-critical representations and attention allocation to relevant content in the prompt, and these representational changes are correlated with behavioral gains.
papers.key_findings:
ICL leads to changes in prompt embedding similarity matrices to better encode task-critical information, which in turn improves behavior.
ICL increases the decodability of task-critical information (e.g., line slope) from embeddings via probing classifiers.
ICL shifts attention to relevant content in the prompt (increased attention ratio to informative parts), which correlates with behavioral improvement.
These representational changes are consistent across multiple layers (except the first) in both Llama-2 and Vicuna models.
The proposed methods (RSA and ARA) provide scalable tools for analyzing latent representations in large language models.
future_direction: Study the effects of ICL on improving planning behavior in LLMs by analyzing latent representations before and after ICL in planning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable performance improvement through in-context learning (ICL) by leveraging task-specific examples in the input. However, the mechanisms behind this improvement remain elusive. In this work, we investigate how LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context-learning, and how these changes mediate improvement in behavior. We employ neuroscience-inspired techniques such as representational similarity analysis (RSA) and propose novel methods for parameterized probing and measuring ratio of attention to relevant vs. irrelevant information in Llama-2 70B and Vicuna 13B. We designed two tasks with a priori relationships among their conditions: linear regression and reading comprehension. We formed hypotheses about expected similarities in task representations and measured hypothesis alignment of LLM representations before and after ICL as well as changes in attention. Our analyses revealed a meaningful correlation between improvements in behavior after ICL and changes in both embeddings and attention weights across LLM layers. This empirical framework empowers a nuanced understanding of how latent representations shape LLM behavior, offering valuable tools and insights for future research and practical applications.

papers.title: Revealing the Parametric Knowledge of Language Models: A Unified Framework for Attribution Methods
papers.research_question: How do Instance Attribution (IA) and Neuron Attribution (NA) methods compare in revealing the parametric knowledge of language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified evaluation framework to compare Instance Attribution and Neuron Attribution, showing that NA reveals more diverse knowledge while IA provides unique insights, suggesting a synergistic approach for holistic understanding.
papers.conclusion: IA and NA provide different explanations of parametric knowledge, indicating the value of combining both methods for a comprehensive view; however, current attribution methods are not fully sufficient or comprehensive, partly because they ignore attention layers.
papers.key_findings:
NA-Instances discovers a larger set of unique influential training instances compared to IA methods like IF and Gradient Similarity.
Neurons identified by NA are more sufficient and comprehensive in representing parametric knowledge than neurons from IA-Neurons.
Fine-tuning with influential training instances selected by IA methods does not lead to better performance than fine-tuning with randomly selected instances.
