It motivates us to explore a fundamental question: How do we calibrate factual knowledge in PLMs without re-training from scratch? In this work, we propose a simple and lightweight method CaliNet to achieve this goal. To be specific, we first detect whether PLMs can learn the right facts via a contrastive score between right and fake facts. If not, we then use a lightweight method to add and adapt new parameters to specific factual texts. Experiments on the knowledge probing task show the calibration effectiveness and efficiency. In addition, through closed-book question answering, we find that the calibrated PLM possesses knowledge generalization ability after finetuning.Beyond the calibration performance, we further investigate and visualize the knowledge calibration mechanism.

papers.title: Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty as a Linear Feature to Reduce Hallucinations
papers.research_question: How is verbal uncertainty represented in LLMs, and can calibrating it with semantic uncertainty detect and mitigate hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that verbal uncertainty in LLMs is mediated by a linear feature (VUF) and introduces Mechanistic Uncertainty Calibration (MUC) to calibrate verbal uncertainty with semantic uncertainty, reducing confident hallucinations by ~30%.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that verbal uncertainty is a linear feature in LLMs, and calibrating it with semantic uncertainty through MUC effectively reduces confident hallucinations, making LLMs more trustworthy.
papers.key_findings:
Verbal uncertainty in LLMs is governed by a single linear direction (VUF) in the representation space, extractable via difference-in-means.
The mismatch between semantic and verbal uncertainty is a better predictor of hallucinations than semantic uncertainty alone.
Inference-time intervention on VUF (MUC) calibrates verbal uncertainty with semantic uncertainty, reducing confident hallucinations by an average of 29.6% in short-form QA tasks.
VUFs are consistent across different datasets and models, indicating a universal feature.
MUC improves the alignment between verbal and semantic uncertainty, as shown by increased correlation coefficients.
papers.limitation: The method may reduce correctness rate due to noise in semantic uncertainty measurement, leading to unnecessary abstentions.
papers.abstract: LLMs often adopt an assertive language style also when making false claims. Such ``overconfident hallucinations'' mislead users and erode trust. Achieving the ability to express in language the actual degree of uncertainty around a claim is therefore of great importance. We find that ``verbal uncertainty'' is governed by a single linear feature in the representation space of LLMs, and show that this has only moderate correlation with the actual ``semantic uncertainty'' of the model. We apply this insight and show that (1) the mismatch between semantic and verbal uncertainty is a better predictor of hallucinations than semantic uncertainty alone and (2) we can intervene on verbal uncertainty at inference time and reduce confident hallucinations on short-form answers, achieving an average relative reduction of ~30%.

papers.title: Distilled Circuits: A Mechanistic Study of Internal Restructuring in Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge distillation restructure internal circuits and representations in student models, and how can functional alignment between teacher and student be quantified?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic understanding of how knowledge distillation restructures internal circuits, showing that students compress and discard teacher components, and introduces an alignment metric to quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity.
papers.conclusion: While student models preserve broad functional behavior from their teachers, knowledge distillation causes significant internal circuit restructuring, leading to increased reliance on fewer components and reduced robustness. The alignment metric captures functional similarity beyond output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, leading to stronger reliance on fewer components.
Student models are more vulnerable to component ablation, indicating reduced robustness.
The introduced alignment metric effectively quantifies functional alignment between teacher and student models.
These findings on internal restructuring and reduced robustness generalize across different model architectures (GPT2, BERT, Llama).
Performance similarity does not guarantee similarity in internal computation; circuit-level analysis is essential for understanding functional alignment.
papers.limitation:
The study is constrained by the relatively small set of models evaluated (6).
The component role attribution procedure is manual and could be automated.
The alignment metric could be improved in granularity and interpretability.
The findings are based on specific tasks and models and may not generalize to all settings.
future_direction: Apply the methodology and alignment metric to a broader, more diverse collection of models.
Automate the component role attribution procedure, potentially using interpretability agents.
Improve the alignment metric's granularity and interpretability, and explore incorporating it as a loss term during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses a larger neural model (teacher) into smaller, faster student models by training them to match teacher outputs. However, the internal computational transformations that occur during this process remain poorly understood. We apply techniques from mechanistic interpretability to analyze how internal circuits, representations, and activation patterns differ between teacher and student. Focusing on GPT2-small and its distilled counterpart DistilGPT2, we find that student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, often resulting in stronger reliance on fewer individual components. To quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity, we introduce an alignment metric based on influence-weighted component similarity, validated across multiple tasks. Our findings reveal that while knowledge distillation preserves broad functional behaviors, it also causes significant shifts in internal computation, with important implications for the robustness and generalization capacity of distilled models.

papers.title: Large Language Models Must Be Taught to Know What They Don't Know
papers.research_question: How can we obtain reliable uncertainty estimates from large language models (LLMs) for their predictions, particularly in open-ended generation tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning LLMs on a small dataset of correct and incorrect answers using LoRA produces well-calibrated uncertainty estimates that generalize across distribution shifts and improves human-AI collaboration.
papers.conclusion: Large language models must be explicitly taught to know what they don't know, and fine-tuning on a small calibration dataset is an effective and efficient method to achieve reliable uncertainty estimation.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting alone is insufficient for good calibration in open-ended generation tasks.
Fine-tuning on as few as 1000 graded examples outperforms baseline uncertainty estimation methods.
Training through the model's features (e.g., using LoRA) is necessary for good performance and generalization, especially in open-ended settings.
Models can be used as general-purpose uncertainty estimators, applicable not just to their own predictions but also to the predictions of other models.
Providing uncertainty estimates to users in a human-AI collaboration setting improves their reliance sensibility and task performance.
papers.abstract: When using large language models (LLMs) in high-stakes applications, we need to know when we can trust their predictions. Some works argue that prompting high-performance LLMs is sufficient to produce calibrated uncertainties, while others introduce sampling methods that can be prohibitively expensive. In this work, we first argue that prompting on its own is insufficient to achieve good calibration and then show that fine-tuning on a small dataset of correct and incorrect answers can create an uncertainty estimate with good generalization and small computational overhead. We show that a thousand graded examples are sufficient to outperform baseline methods and that training through the features of a model is necessary for good performance and tractable for large open-source models when using LoRA. We also investigate the mechanisms that enable reliable LLM uncertainty estimation, finding that many models can be used as general-purpose uncertainty estimators, applicable not just to their own uncertainties but also the uncertainty of other models. Lastly, we show that uncertainty estimates inform human use of LLMs in human-AI collaborative settings through a user study.

papers.title: Calibrating Reasoning in Language Models with Internal Consistency
papers.research_question: How can internal representations in large language models be used to calibrate reasoning, specifically by measuring inconsistencies between intermediate and final layers during chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes internal consistency as a novel measure to evaluate LLM confidence in reasoning by examining agreement of latent predictions from intermediate layers, and shows that up-weighting paths with high internal consistency significantly boosts reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: Internal consistency is a robust indicator of correct reasoning paths and can be leveraged to enhance the reliability of reasoning in LLMs through calibration.
papers.key_findings:
CoT reasoning leads to inconsistencies between middle and final layer representations, indicating uncertainty.
Internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths.
Up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency improves reasoning accuracy across various tasks.
Patterns in attention and feed-forward networks across layers provide insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency.
Layer-weighted aggregation of internal consistency finds transferable patterns that generalize across tasks.
papers.limitation:
The study is restricted to decoder-only models.
The analysis focuses on vanilla chain-of-thought prompting, not other complex prompting techniques.
future_direction: Extending the concept of internal consistency to encoder-decoder models.
Investigating internal consistency under more complex prompting scenarios.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various reasoning tasks, aided by techniques like chain-of-thought prompting that elicits verbalized reasoning. However, LLMs often generate text with obvious mistakes and contradictions, raising doubts about their ability to robustly process and utilize generated rationales. In this work, we investigate reasoning in LLMs through the lens of internal representations, focusing on how these representations are influenced by generated rationales. Our preliminary analysis reveals that while generated rationales improve answer accuracy, inconsistencies emerge between the model's internal representations in middle layers and those in final layers, potentially undermining the reliability of their reasoning processes. To address this, we propose internal consistency as a measure of the model's confidence by examining the agreement of latent predictions decoded from intermediate layers. Extensive empirical studies across different models and datasets demonstrate that internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths. Motivated by this, we propose a new approach to calibrate reasoning by up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency, resulting in a significant boost in reasoning performance. Further analysis uncovers distinct patterns in attention and feed-forward modules across layers, providing insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency. In summary, our results demonstrate the potential of using internal representations for self-evaluation of LLMs. Our code is available at github.com/zhxieml/internal-consistency.

papers.title: Mapping Clinical Doubt: Locating Linguistic Uncertainty in LLMs
papers.research_question: How are epistemic signals encoding linguistic uncertainty represented across the layers of LLMs, and are these representations stable across model variants?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Model Sensitivity to Uncertainty (MSU), a layer-wise probing metric, and demonstrates that LLMs encode linguistic uncertainty progressively in deeper layers, with sensitivity increasing monotonically with depth.
papers.conclusion: Encoding of epistemic uncertainty is a distributed and emergent property in transformer architectures, peaking in final layers, and the MSU metric provides a targeted lens for interpretability and epistemic awareness.
papers.key_findings:
MSU scores increase monotonically with depth across all tested models, indicating greater sensitivity to epistemic uncertainty in later layers.
PCA reveals clustering and geometric inversion in deeper layers, suggesting semantic reorganization of uncertainty representations.
Later layers exhibit substantially higher sensitivity to epistemic modals, aligning with their role in encoding abstract semantics.
The pattern of late-emerging sensitivity is consistent across different model families and instruction-tuning variants.
Uncertainty is treated as a high-level semantic feature that is progressively amplified across the transformer stack.
papers.limitation: Findings are based on a limited set of instruction-tuned models, so their generality across architectures, sizes, and pretraining paradigms remains uncertain.
future_direction: Expand to diverse model types, including non-instruct, multilingual, and domain-specific models.
Localize uncertainty to specific neurons or attention heads.
Examine how internal uncertainty signals (e.g., logits, entropy) relate to output confidence and calibration.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in clinical settings, where sensitivity to linguistic uncertainty can influence diagnostic interpretation and decision-making. Yet little is known about where such epistemic cues are internally represented within these models. Distinct from uncertainty quantification, which measures output confidence, this work examines input-side representational sensitivity to linguistic uncertainty in medical text. We curate a contrastive dataset of clinical statements varying in epistemic modality (e.g., 'is consistent with' vs. 'may be consistent with') and propose Model Sensitivity to Uncertainty (MSU), a layerwise probing metric that quantifies activation-level shifts induced by uncertainty cues. Our results show that LLMs exhibit structured, depth-dependent sensitivity to clinical uncertainty, suggesting that epistemic information is progressively encoded in deeper layers. These findings reveal how linguistic uncertainty is internally represented in LLMs, offering insight into their interpretability and epistemic reliability.

papers.title: Confidence Regulation Neurons in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models represent and regulate uncertainty in next-token predictions? Specifically, what are the roles of entropy neurons and token frequency neurons in confidence calibration?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and analyzes two types of confidence-regulation neurons in LLMs: entropy neurons, which modulate output entropy via an unembedding null space and LayerNorm, and token frequency neurons, which adjust the output distribution towards or away from the unigram distribution.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess dedicated neurons for confidence regulation, which operate through specific mechanisms such as writing to the unembedding null space and modulating the distance to the unigram distribution, highlighting the importance of these components for calibration.
papers.key_findings:
Entropy neurons write to an effective null space of the unembedding matrix and use the final LayerNorm scale to modulate output entropy with minimal direct effect on logits.
Token frequency neurons boost or suppress token logits proportionally to their frequency, shifting the output distribution towards or away from the unigram distribution.
These neurons act as hedging mechanisms, increasing loss on correct predictions but preventing loss spikes on incorrect ones.
Entropy neurons are present across various model families and scales (up to 7B parameters).
In induction tasks, entropy neurons increase output entropy to decrease confidence when repeating subsequences.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to decoder-only Transformer-based language models.
Token frequency neurons are identified only in models for which the training corpus is known.
The case study focuses solely on induction.
Entropy neurons might be a byproduct of dropout regularization, as all analyzed models were trained with dropout.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to encoder-decoder models.
Study other potential confidence-regulation mechanisms.
Investigate the role of dropout in the formation of entropy neurons.
Explore interactions between confidence-regulation neurons and other model components.
papers.abstract: Despite their widespread use, the mechanisms by which large language models (LLMs) represent and regulate uncertainty in next-token predictions remain largely unexplored. This study investigates two critical components believed to influence this uncertainty: the recently discovered entropy neurons and a new set of components that we term token frequency neurons. Entropy neurons are characterized by an unusually high weight norm and influence the final layer normalization (LayerNorm) scale to effectively scale down the logits. Our work shows that entropy neurons operate by writing onto an unembedding null space, allowing them to impact the residual stream norm with minimal direct effect on the logits themselves. We observe the presence of entropy neurons across a range of models, up to 7 billion parameters. On the other hand, token frequency neurons, which we discover and describe here for the first time, boost or suppress each token's logit proportionally to its log frequency, thereby shifting the output distribution towards or away from the unigram distribution. Finally, we present a detailed case study where entropy neurons actively manage confidence in the setting of induction, i.e. detecting and continuing repeated subsequences.

papers.title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs compute and linearly represent the truth of factual statements in their internal activations, and introduces mass-mean probing as a simple method that identifies directions more causally implicated in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The work finds evidence that LLMs linearly represent truth at scale, localizes these representations to specific hidden states, and shows that mass-mean probing is an effective method for identifying causally implicated truth directions.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations of truth emerge with model scale, with larger models developing a more abstract notion of truth applicable across diverse inputs.
Truth representations are localized to a small group of hidden states (over the end-of-sentence punctuation token) in the residual stream.
Simple difference-in-mean (mass-mean) probes generalize as well as other probing techniques (logistic regression, CCS) for larger models and identify directions that are more causally effective in intervention experiments.
Training probes on datasets that include statements and their logical opposites (e.g., cities and neg cities) improves generalization, mitigating the effect of non-truth correlated features.
Probes trained solely on text likelihood (the likely dataset) perform poorly on datasets where truth and probability are anti-correlated, indicating the represented feature is not merely text probability.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on simple, uncontroversial factual statements, so cannot disambiguate truth from closely related features like 'commonly believed' or 'verifiable'.
Studies only models in the LLaMA-2 family, so results may not generalize to all LLMs.
future_direction: Why were interventions with mass-mean probe directions extracted from the likely dataset effective, despite these probes being inaccurate at classification?
Why did mass-mean probing with the cities+neg_cities training data perform poorly for the 70B model, while mass-mean probing with larger_than+smaller_than performed well?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have impressive capabilities, but are prone to outputting falsehoods. Recent work has developed techniques for inferring whether a LLM is telling the truth by training probes on the LLM's internal activations. However, this line of work is controversial, with some authors pointing out failures of these probes to generalize in basic ways, among other conceptual issues. In this work, we use high-quality datasets of simple true/false statements to study in detail the structure of LLM representations of truth, drawing on three lines of evidence: 1. Visualizations of LLM true/false statement representations, which reveal clear linear structure. 2. Transfer experiments in which probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets. 3. Causal evidence obtained by surgically intervening in a LLM's forward pass, causing it to treat false statements as true and vice versa. Overall, we present evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements. We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.

papers.title: Representational Stability of Truth in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How stable are LLM truth judgments under controlled semantic perturbations, and does internal representational stability predict behavioral stability? The paper investigates the role of epistemic familiarity in belief stability.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the P-StaT framework to evaluate belief stability in LLMs under semantic perturbations, and shows that epistemic familiarity (familiar vs. unfamiliar fictional content) governs stability in both representational and behavioral settings.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that epistemic familiarity is a robust signal for belief stability in LLMs, and that the P-StaT framework complements accuracy-based factuality evaluation with a notion of epistemic robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Unfamiliar Synthetic content induces the largest epistemic retractions in both representational and behavioral evaluations.
Familiar Fictional content is more representationally distinct and produces fewer retractions.
There is a decoupling between linguistic similarity and latent-space organization for Fictional content.
The stability hierarchy (Synthetic most destabilizing) is consistent across domains and LLMs.
Representational stability under probing perturbations predicts behavioral stability under zero-shot perturbations.
papers.limitation: Zero-shot retractions conflate belief changes with the number of baseline beliefs available to retract, making direct comparison with probing results difficult.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used for factual tasks such as "What treats asthma?" or "What is the capital of Latvia?". However, it remains unclear how stably LLMs encode distinctions between true, false, and neither-true-nor-false content in their internal probabilistic representations. We introduce representational stability as the robustness of an LLM's veracity representations to perturbations in the operational definition of truth. We assess representational stability by (i) training a linear probe on an LLM's activations to separate true from not-true statements and (ii) measuring how its learned decision boundary shifts under controlled label changes. Using activations from sixteen open-source models and three factual domains, we compare two types of neither statements. The first are fact-like assertions about entities we believe to be absent from any training data. We call these unfamiliar neither statements. The second are nonfactual claims drawn from well-known fictional contexts. We call these familiar neither statements. The unfamiliar statements induce the largest boundary shifts, producing up to $40\%$ flipped truth judgements in fragile domains (such as word definitions), while familiar fictional statements remain more coherently clustered and yield smaller changes ($\leq 8.2\%$). These results suggest that representational stability stems more from epistemic familiarity than from linguistic form. More broadly, our approach provides a diagnostic for auditing and training LLMs to preserve coherent truth assignments under semantic uncertainty, rather than optimizing for output accuracy alone.

papers.title: Brittle Minds, Fixable Activations: Understanding Belief Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do internal belief representations emerge in language models? Are they structured or spurious? How robust are they to prompt variations? Can they be strengthened?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that belief representations in language models improve with model size and fine-tuning, are structured yet brittle to prompt variations, and can be strengthened using contrastive activation addition to correct wrong Theory of Mind inferences.
papers.conclusion: Belief representations in language models are structured but brittle, and they can be strengthened via activation editing, offering a path toward more reliable Theory of Mind reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Belief representations emerge in consistent patterns across models, improve with model size, and benefit significantly from fine-tuning, especially in smaller models.
Control tasks and PCA show that belief representations are structured and not spurious.
Representations of others' beliefs are brittle to semantically neutral prompt variations.
Contrastive activation addition (CAA) can strengthen belief representations and improve ToM performance across different tasks.
CAA steering vectors are general and transferable to other ToM tasks, yielding substantial performance gains.
papers.limitation:
The study focused on one dataset (BigToM) and a limited set of model families due to computational constraints.
The approach could be extended to other mental states beyond beliefs.
future_direction: Exploring how different types of fine-tuning influence the emergence of internal belief representations.
Developing robustness benchmarks and new approaches to improve generalization of belief representations.
Directly embedding perspective-taking circuits into model architectures.
papers.abstract: Despite growing interest in Theory of Mind (ToM) tasks for evaluating language models (LMs), little is known about how LMs internally represent mental states of self and others. Understanding these internal mechanisms is critical - not only to move beyond surface-level performance, but also for model alignment and safety, where subtle misattributions of mental states may go undetected in generated outputs. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation of belief representations in LMs by probing models across different scales, training regimens, and prompts - using control tasks to rule out confounds. Our experiments provide evidence that both model size and fine-tuning substantially improve LMs' internal representations of others' beliefs, which are structured - not mere by-products of spurious correlations - yet brittle to prompt variations. Crucially, we show that these representations can be strengthened: targeted edits to model activations can correct wrong ToM inferences.

papers.title: Are language models aware of the road not taken? Token-level uncertainty and hidden state dynamics
papers.research_question: Do language models represent the alternate paths they could take during generation? How do hidden activations correlate with token-level uncertainty and steering success?
papers.core_contribution: Hidden activations in language models correlate with token-level uncertainty and can be used to steer generation and predict future outcome distributions, indicating that models implicitly represent alternate reasoning paths.
papers.conclusion: Hidden activations in language models reflect token-level uncertainty and can be used to estimate outcome distributions efficiently, offering a way to understand and control model decision-making.
papers.key_findings:
Steering success correlates with token-level uncertainty: models are most steerable when they are least certain about the final answer.
Hidden activations contain information about the model's future outcome distribution, as linear probes on the model's own activations predict outcome distribution better than probes on another model's embeddings.
The dynamics of steering success and outcome distribution are similar, with abrupt changes at the same token positions identified by change point detection.
The correlation between steering success and base outcome probability is moderate (R=0.57) and consistent across examples (average R=0.64).
Linear probes are most predictive in middle layers (layers 6-10) of the model.
papers.limitation:
The computational cost of Forking Paths Analysis is high, requiring millions of tokens to analyze a single base path completion.
Only a handful of examples from three datasets are analyzed due to computational constraints.
papers.abstract: When a language model generates text, the selection of individual tokens might lead it down very different reasoning paths, making uncertainty difficult to quantify. In this work, we consider whether reasoning language models represent the alternate paths that they could take during generation. To test this hypothesis, we use hidden activations to control and predict a language model's uncertainty during chain-of-thought reasoning. In our experiments, we find a clear correlation between how uncertain a model is at different tokens, and how easily the model can be steered by controlling its activations. This suggests that activation interventions are most effective when there are alternate paths available to the model -- in other words, when it has not yet committed to a particular final answer. We also find that hidden activations can predict a model's future outcome distribution, demonstrating that models implicitly represent the space of possible paths.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: DistillLens: Symmetric Knowledge Distillation Through Logit Lens
papers.research_question: How can we improve knowledge distillation by aligning the intermediate thought processes of student and teacher models using symmetric divergence objectives?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DISTILLLENS, a knowledge distillation framework that uses Logit Lens and symmetric divergence to align intermediate layer distributions, improving student performance.
papers.conclusion: DISTILLLENS effectively aligns intermediate thought trajectories of student and teacher models, consistently outperforming standard KD and feature-transfer methods across GPT-2 and Llama architectures.
papers.key_findings:
DISTILLLENS outperforms standard KD and feature-transfer baselines on diverse instruction-following benchmarks.
The symmetric divergence objective (JSD) enforces a dual-sided penalty that prevents both overconfidence and underconfidence.
DISTILLLENS reduces exposure bias compared to standard KD without the computational overhead of on-policy methods.
The method is modular and can be combined with existing KD baselines, with the most improvement when combined with mode-seeking objectives like RKL.
Ablation studies show that using 5 interleaved intermediate layers yields the best performance.
papers.limitation: Computational overhead during training due to projecting multiple intermediate layers through the unembedding matrix.
future_direction: Inject complex reasoning capabilities into smaller architectures
Extend to cross-architecture distillation
papers.abstract: Standard Knowledge Distillation (KD) compresses Large Language Models (LLMs) by optimizing final outputs, yet it typically treats the teacher's intermediate layer's thought process as a black box. While feature-based distillation attempts to bridge this gap, existing methods (e.g., MSE and asymmetric KL divergence) ignore the rich uncertainty profiles required for the final output. In this paper, we introduce DistillLens, a framework that symmetrically aligns the evolving thought processes of student and teacher models. By projecting intermediate hidden states into the vocabulary space via the Logit Lens, we enforce structural alignment using a symmetric divergence objective. Our analysis proves that this constraint imposes a dual-sided penalty, preventing both overconfidence and underconfidence while preserving the high-entropy information conduits essential for final deduction. Extensive experiments on GPT-2 and Llama architectures demonstrate that DistillLens consistently outperforms standard KD and feature-transfer baselines on diverse instruction-following benchmarks. The code is available at https://github.com/manishdhakal/DistillLens.

papers.title: The Hidden Uncertainty in a Neural Networks Activations
papers.research_question: Does the distribution of a neural network's latent representations correlate with epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty, and can it be used to estimate uncertainty without modifying the training procedure?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for estimating both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty from the latent representations of neural networks without modifying the training procedure, showing that deeper layers yield uncertainty estimates similar to established methods like MC Dropout and Deep Ensembles.
papers.conclusion: The hidden activations of neural networks contain information about both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. Uncertainty proxies derived from density estimates of deep layers closely follow those of established methods, enabling wide application and rapid deployment without retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Epistemic uncertainty can be identified with the negative log-likelihood (surprise) of observing a particular latent representation.
Aleatoric uncertainty can be quantified via the entropy of the predictive distribution derived from output-conditional latent densities.
Deeper layers yield epistemic uncertainty estimates that behave similarly to established but computationally expensive methods (e.g., MC Dropout, Deep Ensembles).
Shallow layers yield more conservative epistemic uncertainty estimates, which are better for out-of-distribution detection but worse for calibration near the training data distribution.
Additional regularization (e.g., a reconstruction loss) improves out-of-distribution detection performance but leads to ambiguous calibration close to the training data distribution.
papers.limitation:
Feature collapse can make activations of out-of-distribution data indistinguishable from training data.
High-dimensional densities are challenging to estimate.
Additional regularization improves out-of-distribution detection but leads to ambiguous calibration near the training data distribution.
future_direction: Aggregating uncertainty information from several layers for out-of-distribution detection.
papers.abstract: The distribution of a neural network's latent representations has been successfully used to detect out-of-distribution (OOD) data. This work investigates whether this distribution moreover correlates with a model's epistemic uncertainty, thus indicates its ability to generalise to novel inputs. We first empirically verify that epistemic uncertainty can be identified with the surprise, thus the negative log-likelihood, of observing a particular latent representation. Moreover, we demonstrate that the output-conditional distribution of hidden representations also allows quantifying aleatoric uncertainty via the entropy of the predictive distribution. We analyse epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty inferred from the representations of different layers and conclude that deeper layers lead to uncertainty with similar behaviour as established - but computationally more expensive - methods (e.g. deep ensembles). While our approach does not require modifying the training process, we follow prior work and experiment with an additional regularising loss that increases the information in the latent representations. We find that this leads to improved OOD detection of epistemic uncertainty at the cost of ambiguous calibration close to the data distribution. We verify our findings on both classification and regression models.

papers.title: The Language Model Understood the Prompt was Ambiguous: Probing Syntactic Uncertainty Through Generation
papers.research_question: To what extent do neural language models exhibit uncertainty over multiple syntactic analyses when processing temporarily ambiguous inputs, and how is that uncertainty modulated by disambiguating cues?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a generation-based method to probe syntactic uncertainty in language models, finding that LMs can track multiple analyses simultaneously and are sensitive to disambiguating cues, though with some limitations.
papers.conclusion: Generation is an informative tool to probe syntactic uncertainty in language models, revealing that LMs exhibit uncertainty and are sensitive to disambiguating cues, but with room for improvement in certain constructions.
papers.key_findings:
Language models can track multiple syntactic analyses simultaneously when processing temporary ambiguities.
The degree of uncertainty varies across ambiguity types (NP/S, NP/Z, Noun/Verb) and across specific sentences.
Disambiguating cues often appropriately reduce syntactic uncertainty in favor of the correct analysis.
For NP/Z ambiguities, some generated completions show confusion over sentence structure, indicating lingering effects of initial misinterpretations.
For Noun/Verb ambiguities, models sometimes fail to use number agreement cues, especially when pointing to a Verb reading.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on automatic classification using a syntactic parser, which can introduce noise and misclassifications.
Inability to automatically detect ungrammatical completions or those with unclear analysis.
future_direction: Determine whether inter-item variation in model uncertainty mirrors human expectations and/or corpus statistics.
Overcome limitations related to parser errors and detection of ungrammatical sentences.
papers.abstract: Temporary syntactic ambiguities arise when the beginning of a sentence is compatible with multiple syntactic analyses. We inspect to which extent neural language models (LMs) exhibit uncertainty over such analyses when processing temporarily ambiguous inputs, and how that uncertainty is modulated by disambiguating cues. We probe the LM's expectations by generating from it: we use stochastic decoding to derive a set of sentence completions, and estimate the probability that the LM assigns to each interpretation based on the distribution of parses across completions. Unlike scoring-based methods for targeted syntactic evaluation, this technique makes it possible to explore completions that are not hypothesized in advance by the researcher. We apply this method to study the behavior of two LMs (GPT2 and an LSTM) on three types of temporary ambiguity, using materials from human sentence processing experiments. We find that LMs can track multiple analyses simultaneously; the degree of uncertainty varies across constructions and contexts. As a response to disambiguating cues, the LMs often select the correct interpretation, but occasional errors point to potential areas of improvement.

papers.title: Decoding Knowledge in Large Language Models: A Framework for Categorization and Comprehension
papers.research_question: How can we categorize and analyze the knowledge in large language models by considering both correctness and confidence, and how do techniques like chain-of-thought prompting and instruction tuning affect this knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the K-(CSA)² framework for categorizing LLM knowledge along dimensions of correctness and confidence, enabling a nuanced evaluation beyond binary accuracy and revealing how techniques like CoT and instruction tuning alter knowledge structures.
papers.conclusion: The K-(CSA)² framework provides systematic metrics for assessing LLMs' knowledge structures by evaluating correctness and confidence, revealing novel patterns in how knowledge is organized and evolves, which can benefit future model development.
papers.key_findings:
Stronger models are more assertive regardless of correctness, showing higher confidence in both correct and incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting creates synergistic benefits when combined with instruction tuning, improving both accuracy and category scores.
Instruction-tuned models show superior context understanding for external knowledge, with IT+CoT providing complementary benefits.
Higher layers in LLMs encode more high-confidence knowledge, while low-confidence knowledge tends to emerge in middle-to-lower layers.
Rising accuracy during pre-training does not guarantee better knowledge structure, as category scores can initially decrease before improving.
papers.limitation:
Relies heavily on sampling to determine confidence levels, where the number of samples and temperature settings could affect categorization results.
The boundaries between categories, especially for 'Maybe Known' and 'Weakly Known', can sometimes be ambiguous.
Evaluating models through multiple sampling runs is computationally intensive, which may limit the framework's applicability in resource-constrained scenarios.
Evaluation primarily focuses on factual knowledge in question-answering contexts and may need adaptation for other types of knowledge or tasks.
For external knowledge evaluation, the framework doesn't fully capture how models integrate multiple pieces of context or handle conflicting information.
future_direction: Exploring sampling robustness and strengthening theoretical foundations for category boundaries.
Extending the framework to more complex scenarios beyond factual QA.
papers.abstract: Understanding how large language models (LLMs) acquire, retain, and apply knowledge remains an open challenge. This paper introduces a novel framework, K-(CSA)^2, which categorizes LLM knowledge along two dimensions: correctness and confidence. The framework defines six categories of knowledge, ranging from highly confident correctness to confidently held misconceptions, enabling a nuanced evaluation of model comprehension beyond binary accuracy. Using this framework, we demonstrate how techniques like chain-of-thought prompting and reinforcement learning with human feedback fundamentally alter the knowledge structures of internal (pre-trained) and external (context-dependent) knowledge in LLMs. CoT particularly enhances base model performance and shows synergistic benefits when applied to aligned LLMs. Moreover, our layer-wise analysis reveals that higher layers in LLMs encode more high-confidence knowledge, while low-confidence knowledge tends to emerge in middle-to-lower layers.

papers.title: LENS: Learning Ensemble Confidence from Neural States for Multi-LLM Answer Integration
papers.research_question: How can we effectively combine predictions from multiple LLMs by learning to estimate each model's context-dependent confidence from its internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes LENS, a novel ensemble method that learns lightweight linear confidence predictors for each LLM using layer-wise hidden states and normalized probabilities, enabling more effective weighting of model predictions based on context-dependent reliability.
papers.conclusion: LENS is a simple yet effective ensemble method that leverages model confidence patterns learned from internal representations to improve performance across diverse question-answering tasks, offering a practical and scalable solution for robust LLM ensembles.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed Max Confidence ensemble method outperforms baseline methods (Majority Vote and Probability Max) on 5 out of 6 evaluated datasets.
Internal representations (hidden states) contain valuable signals for determining model confidence and can be effectively leveraged for ensemble learning.
The method is simple to implement, computationally efficient, and does not require retraining or modifying the base LLMs.
The approach generalizes well across diverse question-answering tasks, including logical reasoning, commonsense inference, and mathematics.
papers.limitation:
The current implementation is restricted to decoder-only transformer architectures, limiting applicability to encoder-decoder or other model types.
The method requires access to intermediate layer representations, which may not be available in production environments or with commercial API-based models.
future_direction: Investigating cross-task transferability of learned confidence patterns for zero-shot ensemble learning.
Extending the method to modern multi-LLM systems and agent collaboration scenarios.
Leveraging confidence patterns and intermediate representations to enhance understanding of LLM decision-making processes (model interpretability).
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance across various tasks, with different models excelling in distinct domains and specific abilities. Effectively combining the predictions of multiple LLMs is crucial for enhancing system robustness and performance. However, existing ensemble methods often rely on simple techniques like voting or logits ensembling, which overlook the varying confidence and reliability of models in different contexts. In this work, we propose LENS (Learning ENsemble confidence from Neural States), a novel approach that learns to estimate model confidence by analyzing internal representations. For each LLM, we train a lightweight linear confidence predictor that leverages layer-wise hidden states and normalized probabilities as inputs. This allows for more nuanced weighting of model predictions based on their context-dependent reliability. Our method does not require modifying the model parameters and requires negligible additional computation. Experimental results on multiple-choice and boolean question-answering tasks demonstrate that LENS outperforms traditional ensemble methods by a substantial margin. Our findings suggest that internal representations provide valuable signals for determining model confidence and can be effectively leveraged for ensemble learning.

papers.title: Do Students Debias Like Teachers? On the Distillability of Bias Mitigation Methods
papers.research_question: To what extent can knowledge distillation transfer debiasing capabilities between models? Can knowledge distillation train less biased models compared to standard training? What internal mechanisms cause the debiasing behavior change after distillation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents the first large-scale study on the effect of knowledge distillation on debiasing capabilities, showing that vanilla KD often fails to preserve debiasing and can increase student bias, and proposes three strategies to improve distillability.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents the first study on the distillability of debiasing capabilities, showing vanilla KD does not consistently preserve debiasing, and proposes three solutions (data augmentation, iterative KD, initialization) that significantly improve distillability.
papers.key_findings:
The debiasing capability of a model is undermined post-KD; students become more biased than teachers.
Training a debiased model does not benefit from injecting teacher knowledge (KD does not improve generalization).
Although overall robustness may remain stable post-distillation, significant variations occur across different bias types.
The effectiveness of debiasing transfer depends on model scale similarity; similar scales lead to better transfer.
Larger teachers do not guarantee more robust students.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are mainly conducted on logit-based knowledge distillation. The effect of other knowledge distillation methods has not been explored.
The work does not explore the scenario where multiple teachers participate in the distillation process.
future_direction: Investigate self-distilled debiasing, where the student iteratively distills knowledge from itself rather than relying on a fixed teacher, and explicitly guide the student using counterfactual data augmentation during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an effective method for model compression and transferring knowledge between models. However, its effect on model's robustness against spurious correlations that degrade performance on out-of-distribution data remains underexplored. This study investigates the effect of knowledge distillation on the transferability of ``debiasing'' capabilities from teacher models to student models on natural language inference (NLI) and image classification tasks. Through extensive experiments, we illustrate several key findings: (i) overall the debiasing capability of a model is undermined post-KD; (ii) training a debiased model does not benefit from injecting teacher knowledge; (iii) although the overall robustness of a model may remain stable post-distillation, significant variations can occur across different types of biases; and (iv) we pin-point the internal attention pattern and circuit that causes the distinct behavior post-KD. Given the above findings, we propose three effective solutions to improve the distillability of debiasing methods: developing high quality data for augmentation, implementing iterative knowledge distillation, and initializing student models with weights obtained from teacher models. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study on the effect of KD on debiasing and its interenal mechanism at scale. Our findings provide understandings on how KD works and how to design better debiasing methods.

papers.title: No Answer Needed: Predicting LLM Answer Accuracy from Question-Only Linear Probes
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) anticipate when they will answer correctly?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that a simple linear probe on residual stream activations can predict an LLM's forthcoming answer correctness, revealing a linearly separable 'factual correctness' signal that generalizes across knowledge domains but fails for mathematical reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The analysis advances understanding of how LLMs encode self-assessment, providing evidence for a general 'Factual Correctness' direction while highlighting the structural distinctness of reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
A correctness signal is linearly separable in the activation space and generalizes from trivia questions to other factual knowledge datasets.
The correctness direction fails to generalize to mathematical reasoning tasks (GSM8K), indicating a structural misalignment between factual and arithmetic correctness.
Linear separability of correctness is low in early layers and saturates at intermediate transformer layers.
For models that answer 'I don't know', doing so strongly correlates with the probe score, suggesting the same direction captures implicit confidence.
The in-advance correctness signal is strongest and most consistent for the largest model tested (Llama 3.3 70B).
papers.limitation: The learned correctness direction does not generalize to arithmetic-reasoning tasks (GSM8K).
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) anticipate when they will answer correctly? To study this, we extract activations after a question is read but before any tokens are generated, and train linear probes to predict whether the model's forthcoming answer will be correct. Across three open-source model families ranging from 7 to 70 billion parameters, projections on this "in-advance correctness direction" trained on generic trivia questions predict success in distribution and on diverse out-of-distribution knowledge datasets, indicating a deeper signal than dataset-specific spurious features, and outperforming black-box baselines and verbalised predicted confidence. Predictive power saturates in intermediate layers and, notably, generalisation falters on questions requiring mathematical reasoning. Moreover, for models responding "I don't know", doing so strongly correlates with the probe score, indicating that the same direction also captures confidence. By complementing previous results on truthfulness and other behaviours obtained with probes and sparse auto-encoders, our work contributes essential findings to elucidate LLM internals.

papers.title: How Post-Training Reshapes LLMs: A Mechanistic View on Knowledge, Truthfulness, Refusal, and Confidence
papers.research_question: How does post-training affect the internal mechanisms of large language models in terms of knowledge storage, truthfulness, refusal, and confidence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a mechanistic analysis of how post-training affects LLMs internally, revealing which mechanisms are preserved (e.g., knowledge storage locations, truthfulness direction) and which are altered (e.g., refusal direction), with implications for model steering and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Post-training preserves some internal mechanisms (like knowledge storage and truthfulness direction) and alters others (like refusal direction), providing insights for model steering and future research in interpretability and LLM post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations in LLMs.
Post-training adapts knowledge representations from the base model while also developing new ones.
The truthfulness direction is highly similar between base and post-trained models and is effectively transferable for interventions.
The refusal direction differs between base and post-trained models and shows limited forward transferability.
Differences in confidence between base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons.
papers.limitation: Complex, multi-step processes such as reasoning and instruction-following are not well-captured by current mechanistic interpretability tools, limiting the scope of analysis.
future_direction: Design better post-training methods based on mechanistic insights.
Extend analysis to other capabilities like reasoning and instruction-following.
papers.abstract: Post-training is essential for the success of large language models (LLMs), transforming pre-trained base models into more useful and aligned post-trained models. While plenty of works have studied post-training algorithms and evaluated post-training models by their outputs, it remains understudied how post-training reshapes LLMs internally. In this paper, we compare base and post-trained LLMs mechanistically from four perspectives to better understand post-training effects. Our findings across model families and datasets reveal that: (1) Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations, and it adapts knowledge representations from the base model while developing new knowledge representations; (2) Both truthfulness and refusal can be represented by vectors in the hidden representation space. The truthfulness direction is highly similar between the base and post-trained model, and it is effectively transferable for interventions; (3) The refusal direction is different between the base and post-trained models, and it shows limited forward transferability; (4) Differences in confidence between the base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons. Our study provides insights into the fundamental mechanisms preserved and altered during post-training, facilitates downstream tasks like model steering, and could potentially benefit future research in interpretability and LLM post-training. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/HZD01/post-training-mechanistic-analysis.

papers.title: Inspecting and Editing Knowledge Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we map natural language statements to fact encodings in an LM's internal representations to enable editing and probing of knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: REMEDI is a method that learns to map natural language statements to fact encodings in LM representations, enabling both editing of knowledge (by adding vectors to hidden representations) and probing of existing knowledge.
papers.conclusion: REMEDI links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.
papers.key_findings:
REMEDI can patch errors made by an LM and insert new facts with or without context provided in the prompt.
REMEDI can help detect errors before generation by comparing edit vectors to unedited representations.
REMEDI increases accuracy on occupation classification and factual editing tasks compared to prompting baselines.
REMEDI generalizes from out-of-context training to in-context editing, suggesting unified representation of background and contextual knowledge.
REMEDI edits preserve correlations between features (e.g., adding 'made of metal' increases probability of 'shiny').
papers.limitation:
REMEDI can occasionally lead to disfluent or incorrect generations.
REMEDI sometimes damages the essence of the entity (e.g., making Wiener schnitzel an anime instead of a food).
REMEDI can also cause unrelated facts to change (e.g., changing the air dates of a TV show).
future_direction: Developing controlled generation interfaces that allow direct steering of model behavior in representation space.
Building tools for monitoring and controlling language generation by directly specifying facts and situations in an LM's native encoding scheme.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) represent facts about the world described by text. Sometimes these facts derive from training data (in most LMs, a representation of the word "banana" encodes the fact that bananas are fruits). Sometimes facts derive from input text itself (a representation of the sentence "I poured out the bottle" encodes the fact that the bottle became empty). We describe REMEDI, a method for learning to map statements in natural language to fact encodings in an LM's internal representation system. REMEDI encodings can be used as knowledge editors: when added to LM hidden representations, they modify downstream generation to be consistent with new facts. REMEDI encodings may also be used as probes: when compared to LM representations, they reveal which properties LMs already attribute to mentioned entities, in some cases making it possible to predict when LMs will generate outputs that conflict with background knowledge or input text. REMEDI thus links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.

papers.title: Know More, Know Clearer: A Meta-Cognitive Framework for Knowledge Augmentation in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we bridge the knowledge-confidence gaps in Large Language Models (LLMs) during knowledge augmentation to enhance knowledge capabilities and foster cognitive behaviors that better distinguish knowns from unknowns?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a meta-cognitive framework that uses internal cognitive signals to partition the knowledge space into mastered, confused, and missing regions for targeted knowledge expansion, and introduces a cognitive consistency mechanism to align subjective certainty with objective accuracy, thereby enhancing knowledge capabilities and clarifying knowledge boundaries.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge augmentation is not merely a matter of acquiring more knowledge, but of knowing more clearly what they know and what they do not.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed framework (CGKE + CDKC) significantly outperforms strong baselines across diverse QA benchmarks.
Iterative evolution with two full 'expansion-calibration' cycles yields substantial additional performance gains.
The framework improves the correlation between internal confidence and accuracy, indicating enhanced meta-cognitive alignment.
Ablation studies show that resolving cognitive ambiguity (Knowledge Confused region) is more impactful for expanding knowledge boundaries than reinforcing mastered facts.
The framework demonstrates robustness across varying knowledge grounding states (weakly, partially, and well-grounded).
papers.abstract: Knowledge augmentation has significantly enhanced the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) in knowledge-intensive tasks. However, existing methods typically operate on the simplistic premise that model performance equates with internal knowledge, overlooking the knowledge-confidence gaps that lead to overconfident errors or uncertain truths. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel meta-cognitive framework for reliable knowledge augmentation via differentiated intervention and alignment. Our approach leverages internal cognitive signals to partition the knowledge space into mastered, confused, and missing regions, guiding targeted knowledge expansion. Furthermore, we introduce a cognitive consistency mechanism to synchronize subjective certainty with objective accuracy, ensuring calibrated knowledge boundaries. Extensive experiments demonstrate the our framework consistently outperforms strong baselines, validating its rationality in not only enhancing knowledge capabilities but also fostering cognitive behaviors that better distinguish knowns from unknowns.

papers.title: Direct Confidence Alignment: Aligning Verbalized Confidence with Internal Confidence In Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we align a Large Language Model's verbalized confidence (expressed in words) with its internal confidence (derived from token probabilities) to improve model transparency and reliability?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Direct Confidence Alignment (DCA), a method using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to align an LLM's verbalized confidence with its internal confidence, improving transparency. Results show DCA is effective on some model architectures (e.g., Gemma-2-9B-Instruct) but ineffective on others, highlighting the need for model-aware approaches.
papers.conclusion: DCA can improve alignment between verbalized and internal confidence in some LLMs, but its effectiveness varies across architectures, underscoring the need for further improvements and model-aware alignment strategies.
papers.key_findings:
DCA improved confidence alignment metrics (e.g., Spearman's ρ, mean absolute calibration error) consistently for Gemma-2-9B-Instruct across all datasets.
DCA produced mixed results for Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct, sometimes degrading alignment and accuracy, indicating the method's effectiveness is model-dependent.
DCA reduced the variance in calibration error (σ_ϵ and σ_M) for most models, suggesting it makes confidence expression more consistent.
DCA had mixed impacts on model accuracy: it increased accuracy for Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, decreased it for Mistral-7B-Instruct, and left Gemma-2-9B-Instruct's accuracy largely unchanged.
The effectiveness of DCA appears to be more dependent on model architecture than on the specific task or dataset.
papers.limitation:
The method requires access to internal logits to extract internal confidence, making it inapplicable to closed-source models.
The method relies on the assumption that the model's internal confidence (from token probabilities) is better calibrated than its verbalized confidence, which may not always hold.
DCA can degrade model accuracy because the preference dataset includes incorrect answers, and the method does not directly optimize for correctness.
future_direction: Expanding the method to be compatible with a wider range of model architectures.
Exploring more strategies to improve the alignment between verbalized and internal confidence.
Developing strategies to mitigate the potential degradation of model accuracy caused by DCA.
papers.abstract: Producing trustworthy and reliable Large Language Models (LLMs) has become increasingly important as their usage becomes more widespread. Calibration seeks to achieve this by improving the alignment between the model's confidence and the actual likelihood of its responses being correct or desirable. However, it has been observed that the internal confidence of a model, derived from token probabilities, is not well aligned with its verbalized confidence, leading to misleading results with different calibration methods. In this paper, we propose Direct Confidence Alignment (DCA), a method using Direct Preference Optimization to align an LLM's verbalized confidence with its internal confidence rather than ground-truth accuracy, enhancing model transparency and reliability by ensuring closer alignment between the two confidence measures. We evaluate DCA across multiple open-weight LLMs on a wide range of datasets. To further assess this alignment, we also introduce three new calibration error-based metrics. Our results show that DCA improves alignment metrics on certain model architectures, reducing inconsistencies in a model's confidence expression. However, we also show that it can be ineffective on others, highlighting the need for more model-aware approaches in the pursuit of more interpretable and trustworthy LLMs.

papers.title: Beyond the Final Layer: Intermediate Representations for Better Multilingual Calibration in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Why do non-English languages suffer from worse calibration in Large Language Models, and can intermediate layers provide a more reliable calibration signal than the final layer?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that late-intermediate layers in LLMs provide a more reliable and better-calibrated confidence signal for non-English languages than the final, English-biased layer, and introduces training-free methods (including LACE) that leverage these layers to significantly improve multilingual calibration.
papers.conclusion: The work highlights the hidden costs of English-centric alignment in LLMs and offers a new path toward more globally equitable and trustworthy models by looking beyond the final layer for confidence estimation.
papers.key_findings:
Non-English languages consistently exhibit worse calibration than English across six major LLM families, with calibration error correlating with language resource availability.
While English calibration improves monotonically with model depth, multilingual calibration peaks in late-intermediate layers before degrading at the final layer.
The proposed Language-Aware Confidence Ensemble (LACE) method, which adaptively selects optimal intermediate layers per language, substantially reduces the cross-lingual calibration gap.
papers.limitation: The study is conducted primarily on multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) tasks; the findings may not generalize to other task formats.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to other task formats beyond MCQA.
Investigating the layer-wise calibration properties in other model architectures and training paradigms.
papers.abstract: Confidence calibration, the alignment of a model's predicted confidence with its actual accuracy, is crucial for the reliable deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, this critical property remains largely under-explored in multilingual contexts. In this work, we conduct the first large-scale, systematic studies of multilingual calibration across six model families and over 100 languages, revealing that non-English languages suffer from systematically worse calibration. To diagnose this, we investigate the model's internal representations and find that the final layer, biased by English-centric training, provides a poor signal for multilingual confidence. In contrast, our layer-wise analysis uncovers a key insight that late-intermediate layers consistently offer a more reliable and better-calibrated signal. Building on this, we introduce a suite of training-free methods, including Language-Aware Confidence Ensemble (LACE), which adaptively selects an optimal ensemble of layers for each specific language. Our study highlights the hidden costs of English-centric alignment and offer a new path toward building more globally equitable and trustworthy LLMs by looking beyond the final layer.

papers.title: Interpreting and Mitigating Unwanted Uncertainty in LLMs
papers.research_question: What internal mechanisms cause LLMs to flip from correct to incorrect answers under re-evaluation, and how can we intervene to mitigate this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a small set of non-retrieval attention heads that cause unwanted uncertainty in LLMs and shows that targeted masking of these heads reduces flip behavior by up to 15% without harming baseline accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Unwanted uncertainty in LLMs is not a byproduct of retrieval failure, but rather a consequence of specific attention heads that influence decision-making under re-evaluation; masking these heads can reduce flip behavior while preserving overall accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Retrieval heads are not primarily responsible for avoiding uncertainty.
A small set of non-retrieval attention heads disproportionately attend to misleading tokens in uncertain contexts.
Masking these heads reduces flip behavior by up to 15% without introducing incoherence or overcorrection.
Masking uncertainty heads is effective only in cases of low uncertainty and can lead to overconfidence in incorrect answers in high-uncertainty tasks.
There exist some non-retrieval heads responsible for coherent outputs.
papers.limitation: Masking uncertainty heads can increase overconfidence in incorrect predictions in high-uncertainty tasks.
future_direction: Generalization to other models, architectures, and tasks.
Identifying and characterizing heads that yield incoherent outputs.
Better uncertainty head detection by analyzing attention head output vectors.
papers.abstract: Despite their impressive capabilities, Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit unwanted uncertainty, a phenomenon where a model changes a previously correct answer into an incorrect one when re-prompted. This behavior undermines trust and poses serious risks in high-stakes domains. In this work, we investigate the mechanisms that drive this phenomenon. We adapt the Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval framework and integrate a Flip-style re-evaluation prompt to simulate realistic answer-flipping scenarios. We find that retrieval heads are not primarily responsible for avoiding uncertainty. Instead, we identify a small set of non-retrieval attention heads that disproportionately attend to misleading tokens in uncertain contexts. Masking these heads yields significant improvements, reducing flip behavior by up to 15% without introducing incoherence or overcorrection. However, when tested for downstream tasks, we observe trade-offs with flip behavior. Our findings contribute to the growing field of mechanistic interpretability and present a simple yet effective technique for mitigating uncertainty-driven failure modes in LLMs.

papers.title: Calibration Across Layers: Understanding Calibration Evolution in LLMs
papers.research_question: How does calibration evolve throughout the depth of transformer-based language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that calibration is a distributed phenomenon across network layers, with a distinct confidence correction phase in later layers, and identifies a low-dimensional calibration direction in the residual stream that can improve calibration metrics without harming accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Our findings suggest that calibration is a distributed phenomenon, shaped throughout the network’s forward pass, not just in its final projection, providing new insights into how confidence-regulating mechanisms operate within LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Calibration evolves across layers, with a distinct confidence correction phase in later layers where models become overconfident and then recalibrate.
A low-dimensional calibration direction in the residual stream is identified, and perturbing it improves calibration metrics (ECE and MCE) without affecting accuracy.
The unembedding matrix's null space plays a role in calibration.
Calibration is a distributed phenomenon across the network depth, not just in the final projection.
papers.limitation:
The calibration direction identified in Phi-2 does not generalize effectively to Mistral or LLaMA-2.
The analysis is limited to zero-shot MCQA prompts and may not extend to in-context learning settings.
future_direction: Generalizing calibration directions using gradient-based approaches and verifying alignment with low-rank structures in the unembedding matrix.
Investigating model internals to identify neurons or components that contribute to confidence modulation.
Extending analysis to in-context learning settings and cross-model/dataset transferability.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated inherent calibration capabilities, where predicted probabilities align well with correctness, despite prior findings that deep neural networks are often overconfident. Recent studies have linked this behavior to specific components in the final layer, such as entropy neurons and the unembedding matrix null space. In this work, we provide a complementary perspective by investigating how calibration evolves throughout the network depth. Analyzing multiple open-weight models on the MMLU benchmark, we uncover a distinct confidence correction phase in the upper/later layers, where model confidence is actively recalibrated after decision certainty has been reached. Furthermore, we identify a low-dimensional calibration direction in the residual stream whose perturbation significantly improves calibration metrics (ECE and MCE) without harming accuracy. Our findings suggest that calibration is a distributed phenomenon, shaped throughout the network forward pass, not just in its final projection, providing new insights into how confidence-regulating mechanisms operate within LLMs.

papers.title: LLM Knowledge is Brittle: Truthfulness Representations Rely on Superficial Resemblance
papers.research_question: Do LLMs learn robust underlying knowledge representations, or are they fragile and tied to the exact phrasings and formulations seen during training?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs' internal representations of statement truthfulness are brittle and degrade under superficial, semantically-preserving transformations, indicating that knowledge representations rely on superficial resemblance to pre-training data rather than robust, generalizable knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LLMs learn shallow, non-robust knowledge representations that fail to generalize to scenarios unlike those seen during training, presenting a fundamental challenge for the utility of truthfulness probes and the reliability of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness separability degrades as samples become more out-of-distribution (OOD) across all probing methods, datasets, and model families.
Certain topics (e.g., sociology, marketing) have more robust representations than others (e.g., history).
Benchmark performance does not imply robust representations; knowledge representations degrade even for questions the model answers correctly.
Larger models may not be more robust; the 70B Llama model showed the steepest degradation in some cases.
The type of transformation affects degradation differently; translation breaks representations while negation does not affect internal probe performance.
papers.limitation:
Analysis limited to decoder-only autoregressive language models.
